speechtext: 1. Has the government any information as to the proposed Imperial Labour Bureau to be established by the Salvation Army, for the purpose of placing homeless and hopeless people where they are needed in the colonies, as outlined in the following article, appearing in the Ottawa 'Citizen' of May 13, 1904 -

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext:
" London, May 12.-General Booth's great scheme to establish an Imperial Labour Bureau, and to place the worthless and hopeless people where they are needed in the colonies, has met with a very favourable reception. W. R. Preston, the Commissioner of Immigration for Canada, described it as a magnificent project.
" 1 It is a workable scheme,' he said, ' and it will go a long way towards the solution of what is known as the social problem in this country.
" * Twenty-five per cent of our correspondents belong to the best class of sober and industrious people. They would go to Canada to-morrow, but they have not the means of crossing the Atlantic.
" * The other day, Lord Minto received a 1 letter from a sixteen-year-old boy, who begged

to be allowed a chance in Canada, as he could not earn enough money in this country to support his mother. This boy's case is now being investigated on this side.
" ' I have long been puzzled to know why British philanthropy, which is the most wonderful in the world, has not promoted such a scheme as General Booth's before now.
" ' Of course,' continued Mr. Preston, ' if the government were to attempt such a project, the expense of organization would be enormous ; but the Salvation Army, working in co-operation with the Canadian government, have their vast machinery ready to hand.
" * Every man sent out to Canada will have work found for him. In many cases of men with small families, the Ontario government has built small houses for the wives and children, anl allotted them a plot of ground for produce raising.
" ' Their legislation enables them also to take away children from drunken or immoral parents ; and the State, in its own interests, looks after these children, and Cuds work for them.
' Even if General Booth's scheme could not be made self-supporting, the matter of pounds, shillings and pence should not be allowed to weigh against the w'elfare, moral and physical of the nation.'
" Mr. Bruce Lefroy, Agent General for West-Australia, said : 'To be a success,-tue scheme must be worked from within, and not from without. That is to say, *he Australians themselves must decide where the men are to go, and what men shall go.
" ' There are,' admitted Mr. Lefroy, ' vast tracts of country ready for emigration, but I am doubtful about the " submerged tenth." It is the man who will not work in this country can be made to work in Australia, then all will be well. In the southwest division of Western Australia there are over 8,000,000 acres ready for settlers.
" ' The great population at the gold fields, which produce nothing from the soil but gold, is dependent upon the coast for all its provisions. Here there is a splendid opportunity for the tillers of the soil. The finest produce in the world can be raised in this southwest division. The cultivation of the soil creates a demand for other trades, but this is the first step towards the growth of a country. Mechanics and carpenters and builders cannot find employment until the agriculturist has commenced his work. The total imports of farm produce for last year approximates to one million seven hundred and [DOT] fifty thousand pounds. This produce could easily be raised locally. There are any number of the right sort of young farmers who would go, if their passages were paid, and these are the men that Western Australia requires ' " ?

The directors of the Grand Trunk Company may from time to time, and as often as they deem necessary, enter into an agreement or agreements with the directors of the Pacific Company respecting the manner and the terms upon which the Grand Trunk Company shall or may aid or assist the Pacific Company in carrying the scheduled agreements into effect, and also respecting the consideration to be given by the Pacific Company to the Grand Trunk Company under the terms of any such agreement or agreements, and may guarantee the bonds, debentures or other securities of the Pacific Company, and perform such other services for the Pacific Company as are agreed upon, and the Grand Trunk Company may receive and take as the consideration, in whole or in part, to be given to it under the terms of any such agreement, shares of the capital stock of the Pacific Company for such amount and upon such terms and conditions as are agreed upon.
And tbe proposed amendment of Mr. Bell thereto :
That section 3 of the Bill be amended by adding thereto the following subclause 2 :-
(2) Provided always that when and so often as any share of the capital stock of the Pacific Company shall be so given to the Grand Trunk Company, or be allotted or handed over to the Grand Trunk Company under the provisions of section 11 of the Act incorporating the Pacific Company, thereupon three of the like shares shall be given, allotted and handed over to the Dominion of Canada in part considera-i tion for the aid given to the Pacific Company.

The propriety of the resolution which I have moved in amendment to section 3 will, I am sure, become very clear on consideration of the fact that the common stock of the Grand Trunk Pacific is apparently intended to be given to the Grand Trunk Company in return for the services to be rendered by that company to the Pacific Company in the completion of its scheme. The capital stock of the company is fixed at $45,000,000 of which $20,000,000 may be made preferred stock and apparently that has been left out of sight in the calculation and arrangements made by the government. It must have been assumed that $20,000,000 of this stock was to' be constituted preferred stock and might be sold or disposed of for some purpose, but apparent-

it is to fulfil the expectations of the right hon. Prime Minister and the government who hold that the result of the building of this great work will be to divert the traffic which at present flows through American ports to our own Canadian ports. It would seem that nothing is more certain than the fact that the Grand Trunk Railway Company would be interested for all time to come in continuing to make the road which they now own, running to Portland, and the terminals which they own at Portland, a profitable property. If that portion of their scheme is profitable, if that portion is to continue earning dividends for the company they must necessarily try to secure for that part of their property as much of the traffic that they are going to gather in the west as they possibly can. I do not think there is any room to doubt the intentions and purposes of the Grand Trunk Railway Company in reference to this matter. The language used to the shareholders of the Grand Trunk Railway Company by the general manager and president was calculated to warn them of the fact that they must secure at once an extension of their line into the fertile prairie sections of Canada if they hope to continue the profits which they are at present realizing from the old Grand Trunk Railway system. It is perfectly clear that the president and general manager, when presenting the matter to the Grand Trunk shareholders, would not be talking about profits to be. earned for the system of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company terminating at Quebec or Moncton, because, outside of this block of common stock, the shareholders of the Grand Trunk Railway Company have no financial interest at all. Their interest is entirely in the property which has been paid for by their money, the property which to-day is represented by the stock which they hold and when the officers of the Grand Trunk Railway Company appealed to the shareholders of the company to sustain the promoters of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company in building a line of railway from the prairies connecting at North Bay with the system of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, it seems to me perfectly clear that when they argued to the shareholders that it was a proper, justifiable and necessary operation on their part that they had in contemplation the diversion of every dollars worth of traffic that they could gather up in the west for the line of the Grand Trunk Railway Company and not for the line of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company at all. So that, it would seem perfectly clear to any one that the policy of the Grand Trunk Railway Company must be to continue increasing the traffic of the old Grand Trunk Railway system, and that there is no possibility of doubt upon that subject because every word uttered by these officers of the Grand Mr. BELL.
Trunk Railway Company, every reason which would appeal to any intelligent man and every condition of the contract points to the fact that the whole purpose of the Grand Trunk Railway Company as far as they have gone into this scheme at all is to aid, maintain, and increase the earnings of their original property.
It seems to me therefore, that so far as is concerned any hope of developing a great Canadian tariff over a great Canadian route terminating at Canadian seaports, the whole object of the Grand Trunk Company must be hostile to the realization of such a hope. To place the control of the Grand Trunk Pacific in the hands of a corporation whose welfare, whose very existence requires the diversion of traffic from the Grand Trunk Pacific to the Grand Trunk Railway, is at the very outset a guarantee that the Grand Trunk Pacific will absolutely fail to realize that object which the Prime Minister and his government have held out for it before this House and before the country. It is my opinion that the government have placed the control of the Grand Trunk Pacific in the hands of its most determined and most implacable enemies, and therefore that stock which will give control over the operation of the company, 5 tead of being given to this hostile corporal on should be retained in the hands of the people of Canada, who are really interested in the realization of these hopes of which the First Minister has spoken. Who has a better right to this stock than the people of Canada ? They are financing this whole scheme ; they are furnishing three-fourths of the credit for it, and if that should prove to be insufficient, and there should ever be danger of failure, the people of Canada will be compelled to implement that credit. The, people of Canada cannot shelve their responsibility upon the Grand Trunk Railway Company ; they must accept the entire responsibility should it come to be cast upon them. If any government should set up the argument that the responsibility was to be upon a corporation made by itself ; a corporation which represents only a very small fraction of the wealth and power of the Dominion, the people of Canada would treat such an argument with derision. It is clear that the whole responsibility must in the last analysis rest upon the people of Canada. The burden is theirs, the whole care of this undertaking from the first to the last must be theirs. If the Grand Trunk Railway Company should prove to be of some value in the management of the financing of the scheme ; if its organization should be of some convenience to the government in securing surveys ; that is simply an agency after all. Therefore it is, that the whole burden resting upon the people of Canada ; in the hands of the people of Canada should remain that portion of the common stock which would adequately measure-inadequately measure I would rather say-the responsibility assumed by

them. The Grand Trunk Company is going to do very little for this enterprise. When this matter was before the Railway Committee, those who had studied the question asked : what good will the Grand Trunk Company do in return for this ; and the answer given by the officers of the Grand Trunk Railway Company was :	we will
give that new corporation the benefit of our experience, of our organization and of our terminals. Well, the Grand Trunk Railway have some very important terminals at Montreal, and they have another very important terminal at Portland, and evidently the Grand Trunk Company had in View at the time, that all they were going to contribute to the success of the Grand Trunk Pacific was the use of their trained officers and their terminals. The Minister of Justice told us in this debate, that there was a responsibility resting upon the Grand Trunk Company for a heavy outlay, and he mentioned among other items, the responsibility for providing the money with which to construct terminals for the use of the Grand Trunk Pacific system. I would like to know where these terminals are to be constructed? The terminals at Montreal are in existence now, and if they were given for the use of the Grand Trunk Pacific it would mean some money value, or if it became necessary to enlarge them, expenditure would be incurred ? But we have no reason to expect that the Grand Trunk Pacific is going to give the use of its terminals without some price. Any traffic that comes over the Grand Trunk Pacific, as distinct from the Grand Trunk Railway, would necessarily pay some rental for the terminals at Portland, but it is not the intention of the government apparently that any portion of the traffic of the Grand Trunk Pacific shall go over that fine to Portland-although in my opinion it is the absolute determination of the Grand Trunk Company that all the traffic they can possibly divert to Portland will find its way there. But where are the terminals of which the Minister of Justice spoke, and as to which he argued they would be provided out of the twenty-five millions of common stock. Does the Minister of Justice seriously argue now, that the cost of providing these terminals at either Montreal or Portland is to be at the cost of the Grand Trunk Company, and if he does not, then there is nothing for which the Grand Trunk ought to be paid by the Grand Trunk Pacific Company. I do not think it is possible to show that any burden of outlay is to be imposed on the Grand Trunk Railway Company for these terminals in respect to which they would not be otherwise repaid. Then the Minister of Justice argued that the rolling stock which is to be provided for the Grand Trunk Pacific on both the eastern and western divisions is to be paid for out of this common stock. We do not know exactly how the Minister of Justice arrived at that conclusion, but we do know that both the president and the manager of the Grand Trunk Company have stated to their shareholders- in such a fashion as I think would probably bring them within the reach of the Criminal Law of England, if it could be proven they had made false statements-they have stated that the rolling stock is not to be provided for out of the common stock at all, but that it is to be provided for by a trust, under which the rolling stock will be acquired, and through which the purchase price, and the interest would be gradually returned out of the earnings of the road. There is no possibility of proving to this House or the country that any moneys for the benefit of the Grand Trunk Pacific are to be taken out of that twenty-five millions of common stock which is to be placed in the hands of the Grand Trunk Railway. As a matter of fact it is treated by the officers of the Grand Trunk Railway as being a certain payment made to them in consideration of their services. These high officers of the Grand Trunk Railway have held out to the shareholders the promise, that they are to be repaid for any responsibility, or for any outlay they may incur, out of that common stock. That being the case, and the fact remaining that the people of Canada are really the true guarantors, who must stand behind the Grand Trunk Company ; who must make good all these deficiencies, who must overcome any failure that may arise ; and who bear three-fourths at least of the financial burden of the guarantee of the funds required by this road ; it would justify the claim made in the amendments offered to this House: that three-fourths of this common stock, which is to be given in recognition of services rendered, should be given to the people of Canada if one-fourth is given to the representatives of the Grand Trunk Railway Company.
When in addition to that we keep in mind the fact that so far as any one humanly can judge, the interest of the Grand Trunk Company will not be in the direction of making the Grand Trunk Pacific a success, so far at least as the eastern portion is concerned, while the hope of the people of Canada is that such a success will be attained, we can easily see that it would be much more important to the people of this country that that stock which will give the power of directing the policy of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, should not be put into the hands of what is necessarily a rival and hostile corporation, so far at any rate as the eastern portion is concerned, but kept within the hands of the people of Canada, who could thereby possibly realize their hope of an allCanadian line carrying traffic from the western part of Canada to our eastern sea-boards. Every reason, both of fair and equitable division of this stock and national interest in this matter, indicates to my mind the necessity of retaining the control of the common stock in the hands of the people of this country, if we are going to realize out of this

great undertaking the hopes which the government have held before us. I therefore move :
That section 3 be amended by adding thereto the following as subclause 2 :-
(2) Provided always that when and so often as any share of the capital stock of the Pacific Company shall be so given to the Grand Trunk Company, or be allotted or handed over to the Grand Trunk Company under the provisions of section 11 of the Act incorporating the Pacific Company, thereupon three of the like shares shall be given, allotted and handed over to the Dominion of Canada in part consideration for the aid given to the Pacific Company
Mr, BARKER. I desire to add a few words to what the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Bell) has said with regard to this clause.
I did not observe that the hon. gentleman referred to one feature of the agreement which distinguishes very materially the aid given by the government from that given by the Grand Trunk Company. The people practically guarantee three times as much as the Grand Trunk do in respect to the western division ; but in addition to that the people undertake to pay the interest for seven years on what they guarantee without receiving anything from the railway in return. Now, the Grand Trunk Company will be in possession of the railway for that seven years, and they will receive the earnings to cover their portion of the guarantee. The country presents them, in fact, with seven years' interest upon the whole amount of its mountain section guarantee. The country not only does that, but it undertakes, if the interest is not earned in the next three years, to capitalize and receive back in forty years the three years' interest. There is therefore a very material addition to the aid given by the country, over that undertaken by the Grand Trunk Company, apart from the fact that the country's obligation is three times that of the Grand Trunk. This shows, if anything was needed to show, the absolute fairness of the proposition that where the Grand Trunk receives one share for entering into a guarantee in aid of this Pacific company, the country, which guarantees three times as much, should receive three shares. We hear, and it was pressed upon the House last week, that the Grand Trunk Company had to furnish terminal facilities for this Pacific Company, and would be entitled to some recompense for those terminals. I would like some hon. gentleman on the opposite side of the House to state what terminal the Grand Trunk is possessed of in connection with the western division that it can give as a matter of value to that division. The western division ends at Winnipeg. The Grand Trunk is many hundreds of miles from Winnipeg. It has no terminal whatever that it can furnish to that western division, and it is in connection solely with the western division that this guarantee will arise. Therefore all this rather loose talk about terminals to be furnished by the1 Mr. BELL.
Grand Trunk does not seem to amount to much when you really consider the true position of the matter. What terminals will the Grand Trunk furnish for the eastern division ? According to the contract, the government will have to pay for those terminals. Under section 15 of the agreement, the terminals are part of the cost of construction of the eastern division which the government of Canada will pay for. Therefore I would like to know what these terminals are that we hear so much about that the Grand Trunk are going to furnish. They have nothing to furnish for the western division, and it is* w'ith reference to the western division that this resolution is moved. Chicago and North Bay are the nearest points they have to the western division. They have not a dollar's worth of property within hundreds of miles of any part of the western division. Therefore there is nothing they can offer as compensation to the Pacific Company for the grant of the common stock. As regards the western division, there is nothing from the beginning to the end of the transaction that the Grand Trunk propose to do beyond guaranteeing one-fourth of the bonds, and receiving all the stock they can get for that guarantee. That is the whole transaction with regard to the western division. As regards the eastern division, the terminal facilities are to be provided by the government as part of the cost of construction of that division. Therefore I cannot see why there should be any objection to providing that the government of Canada, which guarantees three times as much as the Grand Trunk Company, shall receive a corresponding proportion of the common stock as paid-up stock, and on the same terms in every respect. If there should be any distinction between them, the government should receive more than the Grand Trunk, because the government, without any possibility of revenue from that road, undertake for seven years to pay the interest on three-fourths of the bonds of the western division.
Nobody has pretended for a moment that the prairie section will not be profitable from the beginning, so that there is no very great favour on the part of the Grand Trunk Railway in that respect. They will get all the revenue. So far as the obligation goes, the Grand Trunk Railway takes only one-fourth of it, practically, and will take all the profits, while the government assumes three-fourths of the obligation and get none of the profits. There is the distinction between the two. I cannot understand why, if the Grand Trunk are to receive $1,000,000 or $2,000,000 or any other number of millions in paid-up stock as compensation for giving their guarantee, the government should not receive at least three times that. In all the discussion we have had upon the various clauses of this Bill, I have not heard one word suggested why the government should not be accorded a proportionate considera-

tion to that which is accorded the Grand Trunk Railway.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
At the risk of repeating what has been said twenty or thirty times already, I would venture a few remarks in reply to what my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Bell) has said. I need not refer specially to the hon. gentleman's reference to the statement made by the Finance Minister at the last session of parliament respecting the question of the distribution of common stock. His remarks were made with reference to a provision of the contract which ",as before the House at that time, and they applied to that contract. It is not disputed that the government would have preferred that the contract in that respect should have remained as it was, and the House is in full possession of the fact that the change in the contract is a concession to the company. To say, therefore, that what was proposed last year differs from what was proposed this year is not adding anything to the argument and not assisting the House in coming to any conclusion with regard to the merits of the case. My hon. friend further, I think, based the whole of his argument in favour of his amendment practically upon the assertion that the entire financial responsibility for the carrying out of this contract rests with the government and the people of Canada. If I understood my hon. friend correctly, he repeated that statement a number of times, and I am quite unable to see upon what ground he is able to make an assertion of that kind. The statement is true only to a certain extent. It is perfectly true that the road originally will be built out of the proceeds of bonds. Sly hon. friend spent some time in demonstrating that fact, but I do not think that was necessary, because it has not been disputed from this side from the beginning that the scheme of financing this road was that the original construction should be paid for out of the proceeds of bonds-three-quarters government bonds and one-quarter bonds guaranteed by the Grand Trunk Railway. It may be convenient for my hon. friend, in arguing the question, to try and .leave out of consideration the fact that the Grand Trunk Railway assumes responsibility for the payment of the interest upon 25 per cent of the cost of the road, but the shareholders of the Grand Trunk did not leave aside that fact. The Grand Trunk Company pledges its financial responsibility to guarantee the payment of the interest upon second mortgage bonds to the extent of 25 per cent of the cost of the road. If the proposition is not successfully carried through, if working capital is not furnished, if traffic is not found for the road, if the road is not operated in such a way as to be profitable, then who are the parties who will suffer ? Leaving out of consideration for the moment the position of the government, which we perfectly
understand, the Grand Trunk Railway will suffer by reason of the fact that it is liable for the interest upon these second mortgage bonds ; and unless there is a profit 11 be derived from the road, the Grand Trunk Railway has no way in which it can recoup itself. So that the Grand Trunk Railway, by becoming the guarantor of those bonds, puts itself in a position which compels it, as a matter of business, to do what is necessary to carry the transaction to a successful conclusion as otherwise it will lose the interest on the second mortgage bonds which it guarantees. It is perfectly evident that that is the manner in which this proposition was looked upon by tlm shareholders of the Grand Trunk- Railway, and I do not think it is debatable that that is the way in which it would be looked upon by any association of business men. If it were stated to an association of business men, met for the purpose of considering the proposition, that the whole financial liability will be upon the government and that the guarantee of interest on the second mortgage bonds is of no account whatever, they would look on the statement as in the last degree absurd. The Grand Trunk Railway is liable for this interest and its liability can only be met out of the net proceeds of the traffic on the line, so that it is bound to see that the line is successfully operated. That is what I meant when, in making some remarks on the second reading of the Bill, I said that the company was tied to this proposition in such a way that it is compelled to furnish not only the working capital but the money for betterments that -may be required from time to time. My hon. friend from Hamilton says that the Grand Trunk Railway will have no-terminals at Winnipeg which will not be provided out of the ordinary cost of construction. The ordinary terminal facilities, which may be considered a legitimate part of the original construction, will no doubt be paid out of the proceeds of the bonds, but I am speaking well within the mark, when I say-every man who has paid any attention at all to the accounts of the operation of railways will bear me out- that large amounts are required for expenditure on the line from time to time, and that the expenditure begins on a large scale practically from the time the road is opened for operation. Improvements, betterments and repairs are at all times required. The Grand Trunk Pacific will have no credit; it will not be able to go itself into the money markets of the world to secure large sums for the purpose of carrying out these obligations. It is already under obligation to the Grand Trunk Railway for the $5,000,000 deposit put up with the government. The Grand Trunk Railway securities must, at the very outset, be pledged for that purpose, and everybody knows that as the operations go on from day to day, money will be required and the credit of the Grand

Trunk Railway will be called into operation, and it will be only through the credit of the Grand Trunk Railway that that monev can be procured. So that, although it is not set down in express words that the guarantor shall furnish working capital and betterments and all the rest, the scheme to day, as a business result, requires that the Grand Trunk Railway shall do these things and many more things, the necessity for which will arise from time to time in connection with the successful carrying out of this enterprise.
Now, my bon. friend from Pictou suggests as another reason, I take it, why it is true that the .entire obligation rests upon the government in connection with this enterprise, that, if a failure occurs while the enterprise is in course of carrying out, resort will be had to the government for assistance. My hon. friend, no doubt, has in view the fact that that occurred in connection with the Canadian Pacific Railway, and that when the promoters of that enterprise did get into difficulties they came to the government and parliament of Canada and asked for assistance, which parliament at that time gave. Well, I am quite unable to see how the suggestion that such a thing can happen applies to the argument which my hon. friend is pressing upon us. What may or may not happen in the future, what the parliament of Canada may or may not conceive it to be in the interest of the public to do in the future, has nothing to do with this contract. If difficulty arises in carrying out the enterprise, if the calculations made in connection with it should not turn out to be correct, and the promoters should come before parliament and ask for further assist-* ance, that would be a matter for parliament to decide at the time ; and we cannot form an opinion on the merits of the ease until the emergency arises, if it ever does arise. But we know that in the case of the Canadian Pacific Railway the emergency arose from causes which cannot exist in this particular matter. The assistance given to the Canadian Pacific Railway was of a different character. The gentlemen who were connected with that company in the promotion Of its financial undertakings had not, at the time when money was required, sufficient financial resources to enable them to secure the assistance in the money markets of the world that they required. They acquired that later on, and developed such strength that the assistance given by the parliament of Canada was returned in full, with the exception of that portion of it for which payment was made in lands. But the circumstances here are altogether different. It is not, I venture to say, in the least degree likely that a similar state of affairs will arise in connection with the contract that is before us. The Grand Trunk Company, with its credit and resources, will certainly be able to meet the obligations that rest upon it.- The government will certainly be Mr. SIFTON.
able to meet the obligations that rest upon it. So that there can be no serious ground for the suggestion that difficulties of that kind can arise in future. Now, if I understand the real point of my hon. friend's suggestion

the other matters to which I have referred being, I take it, preliminary to the argument which he adduced to this committee in connection with this main question-the proposition is practically this : That in the arrangement that has been proposed by the government and embodied in the present Bill the stock goes into the hands of the Grand Trunk Company, and that stock and the voting power upon that stock remain with that company while the operation of the road is going on, and that the policy in the operation of the road, directed by the Grand Trunk Company owning the $25,000,000, will be of a character which is not in the interests of the people of * Canada, but that the tendency of the management will be, in pursuance of what has been suggested as the original proposition of the Grand Trunk, to divert the traffic of the road from the point at which the old Grand Trunk system meets the Grand Trunk Pacific north oT Norfll Bay. And, if I understand the argument aright, it is to this effect -that, in order that we should be enabled to control the policy and management of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, we should have a majority of the stock of that company ; and the purpose of having the majority of the stock of that company is- to prevent the old company, the Grand Trunk Company, from diverting the traffic and taking it to Portland. For my part, I have no difficulty in answering to my own satisfaction the -argument my hon. friend has advanced. That argument does not carry conviction to my mind, because I have never thought, and do not think now, that the traffic whieh will arise in connection with that western section of the line of railway, the construction of which we are discussing, is going to be carried either one way or the other simply because somebody would like to have it carried in that way. I have always thought, and I think now, that when the heavy traffic of the western division comes down to the point of junction with the old Grand Trunk system, the ultimate destination of that freight will be governed by the fact that we have been able to"give a route over which it can be successfully and economically transported to a Canadian port. And that is the main point to keep before us in connection with the enterprise. If the railway which we propose to construct from Winnipeg to Quebec and from Quebec to Moncton will not enable the company operating the road to transport the traffic to Quebec and the maritime ports more economically than it can be carried by bringing it south to the older part of Canada, and so to Portland. I should not hope that that object would be effected. I should not hope that the enterprise would commend itself to the

judgment of the parliament of Canada. It is because we are satisfied that a line of railway can be constructed over which that traffic can naturally flow, over which it will be to the interest of the company to carry that traffic, that we believe the enterprise will commend itself to the judgment of the House.
There is another point which may be talren into consideration having reference to the argument of my hon. friend from Pictou. The Grand Trunk Pacific Company covenant with the government of Canada to pay them interest at 3 per cent on the cost of the line of railway. Will it be to the interest of the Grand Trunk Company, the guarantors of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, to put the Grand Trunk Pacific Company in default in connection with this enterprise ? Surely not. And, surely, we are not going to debate this proposition that is now before us upon the assumption that the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada is agreeing to place its guarantee upon several millions of dollars of second mortgage bonds as an assistance to the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway with the understanding that the Grand Trunk Pacific Company out of the proceeds of its profitable traffic shall pay three per cent interest on the eastern division, and that is secretly the intention of the Grand Trunk Company to perpetrate a deliberate fraud by putting" the Grand Trunk Pacific into bankruptcy as soon as it can. I do not think my hon. friends opposite intend to discuss it upon that basis. But that is the bare and naked effect of the argument which they press upon the House, as I understand it.
There is, perhaps, one more point which may be considered in connection with my hon. friend's (Mr. Bell) argument. It seems to me that the company which has the stock of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company to the extent of $25,000,000, out of which it has been suggested, very large sums of money are going to be made, upon which, certainly, the company will desire to have dividends, would not wish ro see the Grand Trunk Pacific put into bankruptcy and so prevented from paying the dividends upon its stock. Because, if the direful consequences follow which are predicted and the Grand Trunk Pacific is put into such a position that it cannot fulfil its obligation it cannot pay its dividends and so its stock becomes of no value. It is out of this stock that the Grand Trunk Company is to get practically the only return it can get for the difficulties and financial responsibilities it is incurring-which it is incurring at the present time and suffering from at the present time through the depreci-, ation of Grand Trunk stock in the money markets of England. It surely cannot be suggested that holding that stock, having that
as the only possible compensation for the obligations which it has incurred, it is deliberately going to destroy the value of' that stock by causing the Grand Trunk Pacific to fail in its obligations. It seems to me that the fact that the company has the stock, that it desires to profit by the stock, is one of the strongest reasons why we may look for the Grand Trunk bending all its energies from first to last to make this enterprise a success.
Now, a word as to the details of the proposition which my hon. friend (Mr. Bell) has suggested. I think I will be within the sense of the House when I say that the proposition which my hon. friends opposite have placed before us cannot be accepted as a serious proposal at all, or-as one which if hon. gentlemen had the power to put into effect they would put into effect. What earthly use would there be in the division of the common stock of the company in the proportion of 1 to 3 the government taking three and the company one. That practically means a government line. There is no substantial difference. Such a proposal would be a childish proposal. The Grand Trunk would say very properly : If you are going to take three-fourths of the stock take the whole of it, build the road and operate it.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Exactly. Therefore I say if we are going to discuss a proposition for a government road let us discuss that, but do not let us put that forward in the shape of a proposition that we should not have a government road but that we should have three-quarters of the stock of a road ostensibly owned by a company and that we should draw the dividends on that stock. Do not let us have hon. gentlemen going around the country telling the people of this country that if we had only accepted their proposal the people of Canada would be getting rich by the dividends on these shares of common stock. That is the nature of the proposition ; it is not made seriously ; there is not a business-man on the other "side of the House who would put that into effect if he had the power to do so. Hon. gentlemen would do as we do and say : Either this is to be a company line or a government line ; if it is to be a government line it will be owned and operated by the government, if it is to be a company line the control of the stock will be with the company.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The Minister of the Interior (Mr. Sifton) is very fond of stating just what will be done on this side of the House and seems to imagine that he possesses some instinctive knowledge of what is in our minds. The project of the government is that $25,000,000 of the common stock of this company shall be handed

over to the Grand Trunk and the president of the Grand Trunk has said that that stock is to be received for the support which the Grand Trunk is to give this enterprise. The proposition of my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Bell) is a very plain one. He says, inasmuch as the government of this country is giving to this enterprise at least three times as much support as the Grand Trunk is giving, there is no reason from the standpoint either of fairness or public interest why the government should not hold three shares to one held by the Grand Trunk. The Minister of the Interior (Mr. Sifton) says that is not a business proposition. He seems to imagine that the control by the government of this company through a control of the stock is an absolutely absurd idea. Does he not know that exact precedents are afforded ? For example the British government owns a controlling interest in the stock of the Suez canal and does so for reasons of public policy. It has been held out to us by gentlemen opposite by the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and by the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Sifton) that there is some great object in having the Grand Trunk control this great line of transcontinental transportation. The Grand Trunk has one terminus- at Chicago, and its other terminus at Portland. The Prime Minister, only the other day, stated that he did not expect that the traffic of the Grand Trunk Railway Company would in the future go elsewhere than to Portland; that is the traffic which they now control. He did express the hope that the traffic they would gather in the west in the future from this new line would go not to Portland but to the maritime province ports. I do not know on what ground he bases that hope because if the traffic they now gather up is going .to Portland one would suppose that tlie" traffic- wlTOli they gather up in the west in the future would follow the same line and would also go to Portland as their traffic has done in the past. How would the public interest of this country suffer if the government controlled the policy of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway ? That is a question for the Minister of the Interior to answer. Does he think that the public interest would be less served by having that line controlled .to that extent by the government of this country ? Is there any reason to anticipate that our ports in the maritime provinces would suffer ? Is there any reason to anticipate that the rates would be higher if the government of this country controlled the policy of that road ? So far as the question of policy is concerned it seems to me that the proposition of the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Bell) is not only an eminently fair one, so far as the Grand Trunk Railway is concerned, but is one that is pre-eminently in the interest of this country, because this Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
new transeonlinental line if it is going to serve the peopIeNjTTlTC "west as -well as the people of the east-and we have rights in the east which require to be considered, as well as the rights of the people in the west -if it is going to subserve both these interests, it can do so much better if controlled by the government than if controlled by a road which has its interests centred in Portland. This is particularly the case in view of the declarations of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance, both of whom recognize in the clearest possible way that the interests of the Grand Trunk from every possible standpoint would lead it to send its traffic to Portland if it could possibly do so under the terms of this contract. I have pointed out over and over again, thirty or forty times, that there is not one word in this contract which prevents the Grand Trunk from taking traffic to Portland.
The hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Sifton) says apparently that this amendment would not be a fair proposition to the Grand Trunk itself. He endeavours to explain certain language which he used the other day when he declared that the Grand Trunk was bound to see that working capital is provided.. My hon. friend the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Sifton) may have used these words in the sense in which he says he used them but certainly the context did not point to that conclusion. He was discussing the terms of the contract and any one reading his language would understand it as a plain declaration that there was some term in the contract which bound the Grand Trunk Company to provide working capital. The Grand Trunk is not bound to do that under the contract. The Minister of the Interior (Mr. Sifton) says the Grand Trunk is bound to do so, because it guarantees what he calls second mortgage bonds, and the Minister of the Interior refers even to the interest on these bonds. Has the hon. gentleman read this contract ? Has he not yet awakened to the fact that the bonds guaranteed by the Grand Trunk, so far as interest is concerned, are exactly on a par with those guaranteed by the government ? Has he not yet discovered that in the contract V My hon. friend shakes his* head, apparently he has not. We have been discussing its terms long enough for him to realize that fact. If he does not realize it, let me refer him to clause 7 in the Supplementary Agreement which I think makes this plain. The Grand Trunk Railway bonds, so far as interest is concerned, are exactly on a par with the bonds guaranteed by the government. Therefore, so far as interest is concerned, and up to the expiry of the fifty years' period, they are not second mortgage bonds at all, they are bonds secured on the road in exactly the same way as the bonds guaranteed by the government are secured.

The Grand Trunk guarantees one-quarter of the bonds on the mountain section, and guarantees a little more than one-quarter of the bonds on the prairie section, but any difference in that regard is more than made up by the fact that the government, upon the mountain section, is paying interest for seven years, without recourse, and after that for a further period of three years the government is bound to pay interest if the net earnings of the road are not sufficient for that purpose, and the net interest for a period of three years is to be capitalized. We might also bear in mind that the advance to be made by the government of this country to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, during the period of seven years in respect to the mountain section is an advance upon which the government is to receive no interest whatever. It is an advance to be made by the government. The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company is not obliged to p'ay any interest upon it, except the interest in respect to the period of three years, after the first period of seven years has expired.
My hon. friend says that the causes which made it necessary for parliament to come to the aid of the Canadian Pacific Railway in days gone by with a loan of $30,000,000 will not arise in the future and that there is no reason to suppose that this contract, for the payment of rental of the eastern division would be modified in any way in the future. Does our experience during the past six months lead us to put very much confidence in the opinion of the hon. Minister of the Interior on that point ? Have we not already, before one single dollar has been spent, before any of the work of construction has actually been begun, had the spectacle of the Grand Trunk Railway Company forcing the government, as declared by the hon. Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson) and the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding), to make concessions, which, during the past session of parliament were declared to be absolutely and completely against the public interest ? The hon. Minister of the Interior practically says the same thing. He says : We would like to have the contract as it was ratified and adopted last session, but we cannot have it. The Grand Trunk will not permit us to have it. That is the story of the hon. Minister of Finance ; it is also the story of the hon. Minister of Customs. How does it happen that the Grand Trunk Railway Company holds this government in the hollow of its hand ? TUnt is the position as declared by three ministers of the Crown. They would like to have the contract in respect to these important particulars exactly as it was passed and ratified by this parliament last year, but the difficulty of our situation is that the Grand Trunk Railway Company will not permit them to have it in that way. It declares that it must have concessions, and 100
because the Grand Trunk Railway Company declares that it must have concessions, they, with reluctance, not believing the concessions to be in the public interest, yield to its demand, and the concessions are accordingly submitted to parliament for its ratification. Well, if the Grand Trunk Railway Company can exercise an influence of that kind at the present time, for what reason does the hon. Minister of the Interior think that it will not exercise similar influences in the future ? My hon. friend the Minister of the Interior may say that we have finality now. Have we finality now any more than we had during the past session ? Does he not recollect that the hon. Minister of Finance and the right hon. leader of the government and other hon. gentlemen who advocated this measure last year told us that not one line or one syllable of the contract could be changed, because, they said, it was agreed to between the government and the gentlemen who are promoting that company. They said, we understand each other ; we understand the interpretation of the contract. What you suggest would interfere with the contract as we understand it and therefore we will not permit of any change. There was finality, then, one would have thought, as much finality as the hon. Minister of the Interior claims now ; yet, within six months after the contract had been declared in the most emphatic manner a final settlement of all the terms between the Grand Trunk Railway Company and the government, the government yielded to the demands of the company and made concessions of a most important and far reaching character. Therefore, we have no reason to suppose that this will be final, and I submit that the only safeguard which the country can receive is some such safeguard as that which is suggested by my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Bell), a safeguard by means of which the government and not the Grand Trunk Railway Company will control the policy of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company in future. My hon. friend the Minister of the Interior says that the Grand Trunk Railway Company is committed to the support of this enterprise and that it will guarantee one-fourth of what is necessary for the construction of the road. If the Grand Trunk Railway Company by that means is committed to the support of this enterprise, is not the government very much more committed to the support of this enterprise ? The government is guaranteeing three-quarters of the bonds and it has to do something more than that. The government has to enter into possession and operate the road in ease of default, and that entry into possession and operation of the road without any means of obtaining any title- will undoubtedly commit the government to any expenditure which is necessary for the proper maintenance and operation of the road after such default has been made. Therefore, if you say that the Grand



Trunk Railway Company is committed as a business proposition to the support of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, I say that the government, to a very much greater extent, to a very much more important extent from a business standpoint, is committed to the support of this road and is committed to the furnishing of any such working capital and the providing of any such betterments as may be necessary upon that road. If no default is made the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company will furnish the betterments and the working capital. If default is made it is upon the government and the people of this country and not upon the Grand Trunk Railway Company that the burthen of maintaining that road after the period of default will fall. That follows from the very terms of the contract. Therefore, it seems to me that the argument which the hon. Minister of the Interior has made on that point from the standpoint of the Grand Trunk Railway Company is trebly an argument for giving to the government of this country some control over and some interest in this road, because it is, to a very much greater extent than the Grand Trunk Railway Company committed to the support and carrying out of this enterprise.

Mr. Chairman, we are building a national transcontinental railway and if this agreement goes through as it is now proposed to have it go through, what will be the result ? Our millions will be subject to the stock exchange in New York. The Grand Trunk stock to-day is on the open market, anybody can go and buy it, and those who buy it can control the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. It is as sure as there is a sun under heaven that American railway interests will control both the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Grand Trunk Railway of this country. Notwithstanding that we are calling this a national transcontinental railway, notwithstanding that we are putting millions and millions of the people's money into this project, the day is coming when American railways will control the Grand Trunk and through it will direct this new railway enterprise. We are making a great mistake. We should control these roads. We should keep the stock in the hands of the people of Canada. Not long ago we authorized an increase in the capital stock of the Canadian Pacific Railway. A splendid opportunity was then given the people of Canada of controlling this stock by having it placed in the hands of the government of Canada. We could have got the money at three and a half per cent and we could have made five per cent on our investment. We ought to do that in connection with the Grand Trunk Pacific.
We are neglecting the opportunity, and as a matter of fact we are building, with the money of the people of Canada, a great transcontinental road that any day may fall into the hands of American railway corpor-Mr R. L. BORDEN.
ations. Do we want the Vanderbilts and the Morgans to control this road ? If we do, we are giving them the opportunity, and when the time suits them to take this road they will take it. Then, this road, built by the people of Canada, will no longer be a national transcontinental route but a mere appanage of some of the great American railroad systems. Sir, the people of this country will declare that such a thing is not in the public interest, and they will insist that if their money is to go into this road, the control of the road must remain in the hands of Canadians. I predict here, and I am sure it will come true, that when it suits the great American railroad interests to do so, they will go on the London market buy the common stock which controls the Grand Trunk, and in so doing they will control the Grand Trunk Pacific and Canada will be at their mercy. Is it prudent, is it national, is it good economy for this government and this parliament to be party to any such transaction ? I do not think the government and their supporters can go on the platform and say that their policy is such that although the people have built the road, the American railroad interests may gobble it up at any moment they like. The government has not ventured any defence of their non-patrloitic policy in this respect. I would like some member of the government to rise in his place now, and deny that this Canadian National Grand Trunk Pacific Railway is not likely to be at the mercy of the American railroad corporations. That being so, why should we waste our money in a project, which cannot be justified from a national, from a patriotic, or from an economic point of view ? The same thing applies to the Canadian Pacific Railway. I believe in the nationalization of our railroads, and I believe that we should at this very moment begin to acquire stock in them. We had an opportunity to get a large block of Canadian Pacific Railway stock but we neglected it ; here is an opportunity to get a large block of this Grand Trunk Pacific stock, and let us avail of it. Whenever new stock is issued by either of these two companies it ought tp be taken by the state, and especially so if it is a dividend paying stock as is now the case with the Canadian Pacific Railway. I say that this project, viewing it in this respect, is improvident, unpatriotic, unnational, and against the public interest ; most of all, it is against the will of the people of Canada who are to-day largely In favour of the nationalization of our railways.

The logic of the Minister of the Interior is usually more or less clear, even though his facts be erroneous, and I was all the more surprised today at his display of false logic in trying to show, that the present project would result in inducing freight, when it reached Winnipeg, North Bay or Quebec, to go over the government constructed road, rather than

over the Grand Trunk Railway system proper. His sole reason for this contention was that when the traffic reached these points of junction, the government had provided by this contract inducements to the Grand Trunk Railway to send freight over the all-Canadian route. But the Minister of the Interior failed to point out wherein that Inducement lies. He did not tell us why the Grand Trunk Railway should desert its costly terminals at Portland for non-existing terminals at Halifax and at St. John. The Minister of the Interior was so illogical, that it was plain to all that he himself saw the fallacy of his argument. Once the Grand Trunk Pacific is constructed and the Grand Trunk controls it, the Grand Trunk will take good care that every dollar's worth of freight over the Grand Trunk Pacific will at the first point of junction be turned over to the Grand Trunk Company. Is it hot com-" mon sense that such should be the case ? At Quebec the freight would be nearly 200 miles nearer to Portland than it would be to our maritime ports, the Grand Trunk Company have a splendid road to Portland with fine terminals awaiting that freight, and is it not common sense that to Portland the freight will be sent ? Even if it should pass Winnipeg or North Bay it would be far more in the interests of the Grand Trunk Railway to have that freight sent over their own line, than to continue it on to St. John or Halifax. And still more, why should not the Grand Trunk Company deflect that freight at Winnipeg over its roads in the United States. Anybody who knows anything about the transportation business will tell you that it costs far more to deliver coal away up in the northern parts of Ontario and Quebec, than to deliver it to the roads leading into Chicago. This in itself would be a strong inducement to the Grand Trunk Railway to use their American connections. On a former occasion I took the liberty of pointing out to the First Minister and to the Minister of the Interior, that possibly the only company on the continent of North America, that should not have control of the Grand Trunk Pacific, is the Grand Trunk Railway, because it is the only company having lines already established over which our western Canadian freight, can be diverted from Canadian seaports. If there is any explanation to offer as to this contention I would like to hear the Minister of the Interior give it, because it would seem that on him has devolved the duty of finding explanations and excuses of this policy of the government.

Just a word on the point I referred to a few moments ago. If the Grand Trunk Pacific is liable to be taken over any day by American railroads who get control of the Grand Trunk Railway then the policy of the American roads will be hostile to Canada and Canadian ports. The right hon. gentleman told us that the great thing we have to fear is the abrogation of the bonding privilege ; but I tell him that a 100i
still greater thing we have to fear is that the control of this transcontinental road is now in the open market and may be acquired by American railroad interests. Let me say now to hon. gentlemen on this side of the House, that the best policy on which they can make an appeal to the people of this country, and the policy upon which they can sweep the country is, to declare : that when the Conservative party gets into power, it will be in favour of the purchase of the Grand Trunk's stock now on the open market, and by, purchasing that stock we will repatriate this scheme we are putting through here to-day, and have a national system of railroads in this country. 1 commend that proposition to hon. gentlemen on this side of the House. It is the best proposition to go the country on I ever heard of. It is right on the line of public sentiment to-day ; it is on the line of the national ownership of railroads. It involves a very small expenditure. For less than $50,000,000 you can buy the stock of the Grand Trunk to-day. As I said before, you could rent the Grand Trunk to-day on a guarantee of the bond issue and the payment of the charges, for a dollar a year ; but going into the market and buying the stock to-day, when it has only a nominal value, is the only way we can get this railroad back, and bring about the national ownership of railways. On that platform the Conservative party could sweep this country in the next election.
