Mr. Chairman, the amendment which I desire to introduce at this stage is one on the lines of the discussion that took place a couple of weeks ago, when the question of granting the extension of time for the construction of the western division was up for consideration, In view of the prolonged discussion that

took place on that occasion, the major portion of one day's sitting having been taker up with It, unless the government have in the meantime changed their minds, I do no! hope that anything I can add on this occasion will have that very desirable result. However, I desire to review, in as few words as possible, some of the reasons why I think the contract, so far as it relates to the western division, should not be extend ed for three years, as provided in this amended contract. We have been told by various members of the government that the construction of this road was of very urgent necessity ; they referred particular ly to the prairie section of 1,000 miles, extending from Winnipeg to the Rocky mountains. Various members of the government, particularly the Prime Minister and the Minister of the Interior, dwelt at length upon the importance of this road being constructed through that congested district, which was already choked with 'freight which the present railway systems were unable to handle. The only objection offered by the Minister of Justice against adopting our suggestion to have the prairie section completed within the five years provided in the original contract is simply that he says he has every confidence that the selfishness of the company will induce it, in its own interest, to construct it within that time. He admits that it will be to the interest of the Grand Trunk Pacific people to construct that portion of the line at the earliest possible moment, because he says it will be the best paying portion of its system-in other words, the fat portion, which will be remunerative from the very first day of its operation. If this is the case, and I believe it is, then it is imposing upon the company no onerous condition to require it to construct that portion of the line within the time provided in the original contract. We are not handicapping it in any manner in asking it to enter into a compact with parliament to complete that portion of the road within the time the Minister of Justice states he is bound to believe it will construct it ; and we are not asking anything unreasonable. in view of the acperience we have already had of this company. When we left this parliament last session, we, as representatives of the people, had done our duty in passing upon a certain contract. It remained to the company to implement its part of the contract. We were told that it was absurd to expect that a company of business men would have so little regard for their good faith and their standing as financial men as to break faith with the people of Canada ; and yet thirty days had not elapsed before they failed to implement the first essential feature of the contract, namely, the putting up of the legal deposit. Therefore, we are not justified in taking for granted that this company are now going to do so and so. Last session the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton), who Mr. W. J. ROCHE.
was put up as an expert to reply to the exMinister of Railways, made use of the following language to show why the western portion of the road should be pushed through to completion at the earliest possible moment :
We have undertaken the construction none too soon. I estimate that five years from to-day, with a continuance of the conditions that exist now, the grain products of the Canadian Northwest will have increased at least threefold. The present means of transportation will prove utterly inadequate, and this road will be imperatively called for	We know further
| that the loss, even of a year, in making the 1 preparations which are essentially necessary, would prove to be a most serious matter before this road is ready for business. ... I believe that it was unnecessary to give the company more than five years, for in five years from the -completion of the road the company will be in a position to pay interest on all charges.
I believe that still.
Here is a declaration of a specific character made by the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton). That hon. gentleman states most explicitly that the government would not be justified in extending the time for the completion of the western division from Winnipeg to the Pacific ocean.
I am sure that if he were in his seat now and wished to be consistent, he would have to condemn the government for giving this extension of three years. But of course if that hon. gentleman desired to be consistent in his inconsistency, he would, like other members on that side, uphold the government in agreeing to this amended contract just the same as he upheld it with regard to the original contract last session. But these are very strong declarations of his and this great weight should be attached to them in view of the fact that he was selected to speak as the mouthpiece of the government in reply to the condemnation of the scheme by the ex-Minister of Railways. Mr. Blair. One year has gone by of the five and nothing has been done-not because of anv fault of tbe present opposition but through the fault of the company itself, in having refused to conform to the original contract, notwithstanding the solemn compact which we were assured by the members of the government last session it had entered into. In speaking of the congestion of the prairie section, which was to be relieved by the construction of this line in the earliest possible time, the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Sifton) said :
The congestion during the last year or two has occurred not only during the months when wheat was pressing upon the railways, but during other months when the railways have been choked with cars loaded with general merchandise; and when the wheat season has come on they have been caught with their yards full of cars loaded with general merchandise which even then, before the wheat began to move, they have been unable to handle. While that congestion was not serious in the early stages

of the development of the country, It has now, according to the testimony of competent observers, reached a stage when it is absolutely necessary that effective relief should he given. No person who has any knowledge of the situation will for an instant throw any doubt on this statement, that if arrangements are not made for relieving the congestion of traffic not only in wheat, but in cattle and produce of all kinds for shipment outwards, and in general .merchandise for shipment inwards, and if those arrangements are not made soon, as surely as the sun shines, the greater portion of that trade will go south to the United States.
Yet notwithstanding that declaration made last year, the Minister of the Interior seriously comes down this session and asks us to prolong that congestion and to allow that danger of having the traffic diverted to the American lines to continue hanging over us for the space of three years longer than that provided hy the original contract. The Minister of Agriculture also spoke on this question, and made use of the following language : '
I contend that it is a crying duty to provide for the future trade of our country. By the scheme which is proposed we do provide for the creation of another transcontinental channel of communication, which will be ready for operation five years hence. Were we to delay the inception of this work, I venture to say, without fear of controversy, that we would delay it too long. If within the next five years such a channel of trade were not created, I venture to say that a condition of affairs would arise in the country which would he a menace to our national existence.
My hon. friend the Minister of the Interior had a good supporter in his colleague the Minister of Agriculture. His colleague made a good second in pointing out the national calamity that might befall us should the construction of this line be postponed a day. an hour or an instant, to use the words of "the First Minister. Yet they are both now asking us to prolong that agony three years and have the people of the west submit during that additional period to the congestion of traffic and all the dangers it may give rise to. In approving this ori->
ginal contract, the Minister of Agriculture said:	.
According to the contract that is before the House to-day, the new road ought to be buil five years after the contract is signed. In 1908 then, the road should be built. We may safel believe that it will be a year or so after it construction before it is at its best in the car riage of freight.
Then the hon. member for Welland (Mr. German) thus expressed himself :
So that we have this condition of affairs, that the railway must, immediately after this contract is ratified, begin the construction of the western division of this railway and must have it completed within five years.
Every gentleman who spoke on that side dwelt on the absolute necessity of the western division being constructed at the
earliest date possible, yet we are now calmly asked by these very same gentlemen to give an extension of three years time foi* the construction of that same division. The hon. member for Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis), although not so lengthy in his remarks, was, if possible, even stronger and more to the point. He said;.
The people of the west cannot wait, they have said that for years. They cannot wait and they are not going to wait any longer, the people of older Canada cannot wait.
But to-day we have that hon. gentleman supporting a proposition to make the people of the west wait another three years. He has now not <the slightest objection to making even the people of his own constituency, which he was so anxious should be afforded relief at the very earliest moment, wait another three years for that much desired benefit. The hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver) spoke in much the same terms :
I wish to say a word as to the facts which appeal to me in regard to the necessity for the early construction of this Grand Trunk Pacific Railway in the interests not of western Canada, but of eastern Canada.
Yet, when we are asking the Minister of Justice to incorporate a clause into this supplemental contract, by means of which the prairie section-not the western division, and mind you, Sir, all these quotations I have given this afternoon referred to the western division from Winnipeg .to >the coast-when we are asking the Minister of Justice to accept an amendment which will not at all interfere with the eight years he is giving the company to extend the line to the coast, when we are asking him to accept an amendment *which will enable this congested district in the prairie section to be relieved and secure beyond peradventure the construction of the thousand miles of railway through this most important section of the country, without unnecessary delay, we are told that we are making an unreasonable request. The reason given by the hon. minister for not dealing wnth the prairie section in this way is that he desires to deal with the western section as a whole. He thinks that the mountain section should not be delayed, but neither do I desire that it should be delayed. What I am asking is that it should be constructed at the earliest possible moment, but I recognize that there may be difficulties in that section which are not to be encountered on the prairie division. I recognize that the work on that section may be very difficult and costly, and I am not asking to have the extension of the time on that portion of the line shortened. I am leaving the supplemental agreement exactly as it is as regards that section, but I am simply asking the Minister of Justice to direct his attention to the prairie section, where

this congestion is supposed to exist; and if we wanted a precedent for dealing with the two separately, we have it in this supplemental contract We find that the two sections are in almost every respect treated separately and distinctly. Take, for instance, the payment of interest. The government are giving a bonus of seven years interest for the construction of the mountain division. This bonus, for practically it is a bonus of upwards of $4,000,000, is not granted to the company for the construction of the prairie division. We recognize that the mountain section is to be differently dealt with because of the difficult character of the country, but when it is dealt with differently in its financial aspect, why should it not be dealt with differently as regards relieving the congestion of traffic ? There is also a difference in connection with the guarantee of the bonds. We guarantee the bonds to the extent of three-fourths of the cost of the prairie section, but our guaranty is not to exceed $13,000 per mile. On the mountain section, however, we guarantee three-fourths of the cost without any limit to the amount. Here again we have a precedent for asking the government to deal differently with the prairie section as regards the period of construction. I shall not at this stage touch on the question of location. The Minister of Justice has convinced me that the government are not in possession of information which would lead them to decide where the road is to be constructed. I accept unhesitatingly this statement. I believe that the surveys are in the hands of the company.
The road is to be constructed by the company and the company will locate the line where they please, subject, of course, to the plans being approved by the government. I, therefore, will not press that upon the government at the present time. But I was struck by one expression made use of by the Minister of the Interior (Hon. Mr. Sifton) which, I think, places us in a rather peculiar position. According to the hon. minister the country is to go into partnership with a company that has practically no credit. He says that the Grand Trunk Pacific has no credit other than the credit afforded it by the guarantee of bonds by the Grand Trunk Company on the one hand and the guarantee by the government on the other. But for this they could not go into the markets of the world and borrow money for the construction of the road. Is not that a humiliating position for the Dominion of Canada to occupy ?
Another notable part of the speech of the Minister of the Interior was that in which he sought to convince us that the traffic would be carried from the west to a Canadian seaport. He tells us that the mere wish on the part of one man or another will not cause the grain to be carried from the Mr. W. J. ROCHE.
Northwest to one of our own seaports. 1 agree with him in that. But, what proof has he given that this traffic will be carried to a Canadian port ? He tells -us that, when the grain from the Northwest reaches the point of junction with the North Bay line it will go to Portland unless more economical haulage is afforded to some seaport in Canada. And he tells us that he is convinced that the traffic will go to one of our own ports. But what proof has he ? What single item of proof did he offer ? He could not give us any, for the simple reason that the government have no facts upon which to base an opinion on the matter. They have no surveys made-the hon. minister (Mr. Sifton) himself has told us that much-east of North Bay. We do not know whether we can get a road through that wild part of New Brunswick of sufficiently low grade and easy curves to secure the carrying of grain by this line. How can he expect the people to believe that this line will carry traffic to a Canadian seaport, when he does not adduce a tittle of evidence in support of his statement ? Without prolonging my remarks, I desire to move an amendment. In view of the fact that this prairie section is through a portion of the country in which railways are so easily constructed that the government themselves were going to compel the company to build the whole division, including the mountain section, inside of five years, I think that we are not making a request that will be taken exception to by the government or the company, if we ask that the company be required to complete the prairie section in less time than is required by this agreement. I, therefore move, seconded by Mr. Boyd :
That the Bill be amended by adding thereto the following section as subsection No. :-
Notwithstanding anything contained in the scheduled agreements, or in this Act, or in the Act hereby amended, the prairie section of the western division shall be commenced forthwith and shall be completed within four years from the date of the passing of this Act, unless prevented by any of the causes enumerated in the 10th paragraph of the original agreement as amended by the first paragraph of the supplementary agreement.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In view of the very full discussion which took place last year when an amendment almost similar in terms was introduced, I am sure my hon. friend (Mr. Roche, Marquette) will not expect any extended remarks from me.
There was no amendment last year.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Perhaps there was no amendment. But my hon. friend discussed the matter. Perhaps what I am referring to occurred this session. However, I am quite sure the matter was discussed, because I remember offering a few

remarks on the subject myself. And I am sure tbe bon. gentleman (Mr. W. J. Rocbe) *went into the matter fully with the assistance of his colleagues from Manitoba. The position that I took on the previous occasion, I take now. What is important in the interests of the country is to secure the construction of the western division, from Winnipeg to the Pacific coast at the earliest possible moment. And, while we have fixed eight years as the period within which the company may construct it, our anticipation is that the company will finish it within a shorter period than that. It is desirable that the road should be constructed in its entirety. We want an eastern outlet, it is true, but we want a western cutlet, for the products of Manitoba and the Northwest ; and I think we can best secure the completion of the road by not adopting the amendment suggested by my hon. friend. Obviously the object which the Grand Trunk Pacific have in view is to reach the rich farming lands of Manitoba and the Northwest Territory. They will put forward every effort to reach that part of the country. It is certain they will not allow an hour to pass in idleness which can be usefully employed in that direction. When they reach that part of the country they will have expended a large sum of money, necessarily. And, it must be borne in mind that under the contract as we have it, they will not be entitled to the issue of their bonds and the final endorsation by the government of their permanent issue until the road is constructed to the Pacific ocean ; so all the money expended in connection with opening Manitoba and the Northwest Territories will remain idle until they have extended the road to the Pacific. It is to our interest to make that situation such that it will be an object to them to reach the Pacific ocean as soon as possible, and we accomplish that by declaring that they shall get the government assistance when the whole road is completed. I do not think it is necessary to say anything further. Our desire is to treat the western division as we treat the eastern division-as a unit. The western division must be dealt with as a whole by the company, as the eastern division will be dealt with as a whole by the government.
I understand that the government do not intend to give any guarantee of bonds until the road is completed^

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I beg the hon. gentleman's (Mr. Haggart) pardon, I try to avoid making rash statements. I said that by law we are not under any obligation to endorse the permanent issue of the bonds until the road is completed to the Pacific coast.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Fitzpatrick) led the House to believeat least the inference I drew from what he said, and, I think the House drew the same inference-was that the government did not intend to make any advances until the completion of the road.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I did not say that.

What we want to know Is whether the government intend to guarantee the interim bonds. And if they do guarantee them is that not giving them assistance toward the construction of the road just as much as if they guaranteed the permanent bonds before the completion of the work ? We have never had a financial statement as to what the government intend to do. Surely that is something the country has a right to expect ? The statement of the Minister of Justice would lead one to believe that, as the government were not legally bound to give assistance before the completion of the road, they would not do more than they were legally bound to do, and would not give a cent of assistance until the company finished the work of construction. For my part, I cannot understand how they are going to finance the road. The company have eight years within which to finish the road. Will the government withhold assistance until the end of that time, or will they guarantee the interim bonds or give any advance ? Surely, that is a financial question concerning which the country has a right to some answer from the government ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am not responsible for the inferences which my hon. friend may draw from my words. I am responsible for my words and for the ordinary construction placed upon them. My position is that under the contract the government is under no obligation to guarantee the permanent issue of bonds until the road had been completed from Winnipeg to Port Simpson. That is what I said. In addition to that there is a faculty or option with the government, pending the construction, to guarantee interim bonds or to give assistance to the Grand Trunk to aid in the construction of the road during that period. My hon. friend will realize there is a vest amount of difference between an obligation to do a thing and a faculty to do it, and the control we can exercise over the Grand Trunk Pacific during the course of construction is very much greater than that which we can exercise after the legal obligation to guarantee arrives. What I said was that the company cannot be considered as having a title to the guarantee of the government until such time as the road is permanently completed from end to end, and pending construction the aid to be given to the company by the government will be dependent, no matter what government may be in power, upon the

progress that is being made by the company in its works, and it would be the object and the desire, I am quite satisfied, of any government no matter which government is in power, notwithstanding the delay of eight years that the company shall execute that work with the shortest possible delay. It will be to the interest of the company to execute the works so far as Manitoba and the Northwest are concerned as rapidly as possible and to have the bonds guaranteed at the earliest possible moment, it will be to their interest to complete the mountain section as quickly as possible.

If you are going to give them assistance in the form of bonds, it will be done on progress estimates as the work proceeds ; you are to give them advances as the woi'k proceeds. If you have an arrangement with the company to pay them on progress estimates a certain percentage as the work proceeds, what is the effect of the statement that the government are only legally bound to endorse the bonds at the end of 8 years ? You are either in the position that you will not endorse them, until the end of 8 years, or you are in the position that before the company go on to construct the road, they shall have an advance on interim bonds on progress estimates. In other words you intend to pay them within 15 per cent of the actual amount that will be obligated at the end of 8 years. What we want is a final statement of the whole financial proposition, how the government intend to act during the construction of the road and how they intend to assist in the building of branch roads to get to Lake Superior, North Bay and Montreal. We are kept altogether in the dark, we have the bare Act of parliament. The Minister of Justice simply gave to the House his belief as to the legal position of the advances which the government makes to the company. The Grand Trunk will not commence to construct a road unless they have an arrangement to get progress estimates and it is right they should get that. They will wish to get the power to issue interim bonds and we are entitled to a plain statement of the amount they are to receive and of the whole financial arrangement.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Haggart) is very anxious to forecast the intentions of the government. I am limited to the contract. Section 36 tells us :
Notwithstanding any of the provisions of this agreement, interim bonds of the company secured by first mortgage may, from time to time, during, and for the purposes of the work of constructing the said western division, be issued by the company and guaranteed by the government, as may be agreed upon from time to time

There is no provision here for interim or progress estimates.
-subject to all the limitations and conditions imposed by this agreement ; provided, how-Mr. FITZPATRICK.
ever, that all such interim bonds shall be issued upon such terms that, upon the completion of the said western division, the same, or so much thereof (principal and interest) as may be then outstanding, shall be convertible, as against the holders thereof, into bonds issued under the provisions of paragraph twenty-eight thereof.
My argument is that these words, as clearly as words can express it, leave it to the government to determine a basis on which the bonds are to be issued and interim assistance given. The government should decide that, and I venture the prediction that the government will decide that in view of the interests of the country and in view of the progress being made by the company.

I do not think the committee will at all object to the hon. gentleman stating that he feels bound only by the conditions of the contract. In the first place the Grand Trunk has eight years in which to construct the prairie section. Surely the hon. gentleman would not withhold the sanction of the government to the interim bonds when there was no violation of the contract on the part of the company. I would like to ask, for the purpose of shortening this discussion, if the hon. gentleman would feel justified in withholding the endorsement of the government to the interim bonds unless they had violated their contract by not constructing the prairie section within eight years. The hon. gentleman says it rests altogether with the government, but the Grand Trunk Pacific on the one hand has taken the power to issue interim bonds ; the government has taken power to guarantee them. We would like to ask the Minister of Justice if he would feel justified in the face of the Grand Trunk Pacific not having violated their agreement to withhold endorsa-tion to these Interim bonds, and on what conditions he would feel justified in withholding them.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: So far as one can speak now of events that may occur 4 or 5 years hence, I would say, speaking for myself, that if I were a member of a government called upon to decide the question, I should be disposed to consider that I was under a moral obligation to assist the company if they had complied with all the terms of the contract, but that the measure of that assistance would be determined by the progress they were making.

I do not understand what construction the minister puts on his own Act, but it seems to me that a common sense construction of it would indicate that it was the intention of the company to issue bonds from time to time as required and that it was the duty of the government to guarantee them.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Without any restriction ?
No, not without any restriction, but simply with this restriction that they would only be assisted in proportion to the amount of road built, and having regard to the full cost of the road.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Where is the authority for that ?

In section 36.
Notwithstanding any of the provisions of this agreement, interim bonds of the company secured by first mortgage may, from time to time, during, and for the purposes of the work of constructing the said western division, be issued by the company and guaranteed by the government,

That is for construction.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Read on, if you please.

-as may be agreed upon from time to time, subject to all the limitations and conditions imposed by this agreement ; provided, however, that all such interim bonds shall be issued upon such terms that, upon the completion of the said western division, the same, or so much thereof (principal and interest) as may be then outstanding, shall be convertible, as against the holders thereof, into bonds issued under the provisions of paragraph twenty-eight hereof.
Now, what does paragraph 28 of the original agreement say ?
For the purpose of aiding the company in the construction of the western division, the government shall guarantee payment of the principal and interest of an issue of bonds to be made by the company

I assume the company would make that issue of bonds for the purposes of construction as they went along, and that the government are bound to guarantee them.
-for a principal amount equal to seventy-five per centum of the cost of construction of the said division as defined and ascertained in accordance with the provisions of paragraph eighteen hereof hut such principal amount shall not, in any case, exceed thirteen thousand dollars per mile of the mileage of the prairie section, nor thirty thousand dollars per mile of the mileage of the mountain section although seventy-five per centum of such cost of construction may have exceeded the said respective sums per mile.
It seems to me that the spirit of that clause is simply that the government have consented to the company issuing their bonds for the purpose of constructing their railway, and that the government have to guarantee these bonds. What is the use of the company issuing the bonds and of the government guaranteeing them if the company cannot sell the bonds to pay the cost of construction ? I think that under the contract the company would be quite entitled to expect that the government would come to their aid to the extent of guaranteeing their bonds and allowing them to sell these bonds
to raise the money to construct the road. The hon. Minister of Justice says that it is distinctly understood and expected that this road will be built at the very earliest date, that it will be built long before the expiration of the time required for the completion of the whole road. That is the expectation, intention and aim. Then, if that is the expectation, intention and aim, what reason is there for refusing to put this provision into the Act ? It is not embarrassing to the company in any way ; it is not interfering with the rights of the government in any way, but it is doing for the western people what the western people desire should be done, and it is fulfilling one of the most urgent reasons that the government gave when they asked the country to make this huge expenditure, viz., providing a railway at the earliest possible moment to carry out the products of that western country required by the rapid settlement and increasing production of grain. Now, then, in all human probability the western division will be built long before the eastern division is ready for traffic. I think it is expected by every one that the western division-at least that portion between Winnipeg and the Rocky mountains-will be built long before the eastern division is ready for traffic. The object of the Grand Trunk Railway has been apparent from the outset. What is it ? To get connection between North Bay and Winnipeg at the earliest possible moment, so that when that portion of the road between Winnipeg and the Rocky mountains is completed they may be prepared to handle the produce that is gathered up along that line. They do not aim at gathering the products of that western country along the line of the western division and handing them over to the eastern division, but they aim at reaching Lake Superior and Port Arthur, or at reaching North Bay. They aim at reaching a port on the great inland lakes, so that these products may be carried forward to one of the ports with which the Grand Trunk Railway system has connection-Midland, Coll-ingwood, Meaford, or any of those other ports that the Grand Trunk Railway Company are hauling grain from to-day. Their object would be to build that western prairie section at the earliest possible date, not waiting until the whole line is constructed, because, if they did so, others would occupy the ground before them. Taking into account the rapidity with which the Canadian Pacific Railway was built when they were laying down four miles of track a day, building though prairie country, we must naturally come to the conclusion that it will only take a very short time to build the prairie section of this road. There are about 1,000 miles of it. If they were laying down four miles a day through the prairie country, it would only take them about a year to complete the work. This amendment says that it shall be constructed within four years. Is that an unreasonable time ? Not at all. If

they aim to build it, as the hon. Minister of Justice says, at the earliest possible moment we give them plenty of time in which to do it If they intend to do it, they will do it within that time, and there will be no objection to tacking on this amendment to this clause. It is a very easy matter for them to fulfil the conditions of this amendment, and if the western division will be ready long before the eastern division, it is not imposing any onerous obligations upon them to' say that they shall build this road within four years, because I assume that they will be able to reach the lake with the traffic which they will gather up after they have commenced operating the prairie portion of the western division.

My hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Roche) has raised the question of the relief of the people of Manitoba, and the hon. Minister of Justice has raised the question of the early construction of the western division of this line. Now, as I take it, the contention of my hon. friend from Marquette is that the people of Manitoba and the Northwest Territories are in immediate need of railway relief. They want relief of two kinds ; they want relief in the way of facilities and they want relief in the way of rates. How could relief be granted to the west in the way of facilities? Immediate relief could be granted to the west by the extension of the Intercolonial Railway to Georgian bay and by the nationalization of either the Mackenzie & Mann system or the Canadian Pacific Railway between Port Arthur and Winnipeg, i By>
adopting that policy you could put the Grand Trunk Railway into Winnipeg to-morrow, and by putting the Grand Trunk Railway into Winnipeg to-morrow you would call into existence a powerful system immediately competitive with and regulative of the Canadian Pacific Railway. That would give immediate relief to the people of the Northwest Territories. Another way to give immediate relief to the people of the Northwest Territories is to have the courage to tackle the Canadian Pacific Railway. There is a provision in the law for the regulation of the rates charged upon that road, but this parliament seems to be afraid to enforce the law. We could ask the Canadian Pacific Railway to produce their books so as to see what that road cost, and, ascertaining the cost of the road, we could immediately call on them, providing the cost was a certain amount and the earnings a certain amount, to grant relief to the people of the Northwest Territories. So, in two years we could grant immediate relief in the way of facilities and rates, but we are taking a roundabout way, and no relief is to be given for at least eight years.
Now, let us take the other question raised bj the hon. Minister of Justice. He wishes to see the early construction of the western portion of this road. How could that be accomplished ? It could be brought about Mr. SPROULE.
on the lines I have suggested, by putting the Grand Trunk Railway into Winnipeg, by using the Canada Atlantic Railway for the purpose of extending the Intercolonial Railway and nationalizing the Canadian Pacific Railway or the Mackenzie and Mann road between Port Arthur and Winnipeg.
If you were to do that, you could put all the energies of the Grand Trunk Pacific into the construction of the western section, and you could abandon for the present the back road from Winnipeg to Moncton, for which there is no immediate urgent demand. Let us put all our energy into granting some kind of relief to the people of the west, and then we will accomplish something. As things are now, we are accomplishing nothing. This government scheme affords no immediate relief to the people of the Northwest either in facilities, or in the reduction of rates, and yet that is what the people of the Northwest are asking for. The government have not the courage to nationalize even a portion of the railroads of this country, and they have not the courage to tackle the Canadian Pacific Railway and force them to reduce their rates. All these schemes proposed here to-day are in the air ; they afford no solution of the transportation problem. The solution of the transportation problem is the reduction of rates, and an increase of facilities for the great body of the people of this country who are using the railroads. We are putting all our energy into building a railroad through a wilderness; let us put our energy into increasing the facilities1 between the Ontario system and the Manitoba system, and reducing railroad rates. Why is the Minister of the Interior afraid to tackle the Canadian Pacific Railway ? He knows that clause in the original Act [DOT] of the Canadian Pacific Railway that entitles the people of the west to relief from the present high rates, but he sits there mum, and has not a word to say respecting it. He has never pressed upon his colleagues to execute that provision in the law by which the people in the west can bo relieved. His idea is, that the relief for grievances in this country is to expend more of the people's money and hand more railways over to private corporations, the only result of which will be to increase the monopolies which already exist. There is no attempt in this Bill to grant relief to the people of Manitoba ; there is no attempt to reduce existing freight rates, but there is a grand effort to give away $150,000,000 of the people's money to another of the private corporations, so as to increase the monopolies that already burden us. That is the sum and substance of this measure. If we are to have a road from Winnipeg to Moncton, and some time I hope we may require to,* well and good ; but our duty at the present time is to make some real effort to solve the transportation problem.
Does the hon. gentleman advocate the suspension of the eastern division ?

I certainly do in view of the fact that there is no call now in the east for railway facilities, and I assert that the construction of the eastern division will have no beneficial effect on the transportation problem. It will not compel a reduction in existing rates which the people of Quebec and Ontario to-day require. The hon. gentleman from Halifax is proposing relief for people who do not jet live in the wilderness through which the eastern extension may be built, but what I advocate is, relief for the people who already are settled in this country, and who have been long oppressed by railway monopolies. Immediate relief for the people in the west will be secured by increasing existing facilities jin the west, coupling the western roads with the existing railways in Ontario and Quebec, and above all, coupling them with our present national read, the Intercolonial Railway. I want to see the maritime provinces have everything * in the way of railway facilities that they possibly can be entitled to, and if this road from Winnipeg to Moncton should become necessary eventually, I would be glad to see it constructed. But to-day it is not urgently necessary. It is only a colonization scheme at best, and it has no part at the present moment in the solution of the Canadian transportation problem. It is going to open up a new country, rich in forests rich in mining, and I hope, rich in farming lands-

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Hear, hear.

Yes, but the necessity for it is not immediate. The immediate requirements of the country to-day, are to increase the facilities in the west, and above ali. to regulate rates. The way to regulate rates, is to put the Grand Trunk into Winnipeg to-morrow-I have told you how it can be done-and to proceed to regulate the rates on the Canadian Pacific Railway. The Canadian Pacific Railway is entitled to give the people of the Northwest relief, and they are not doing it because of lack of courage on the part of the government, and especially lack of courage on the part of the Minister of the Interior. He lias not raised his voice once against the monopolistic clause of the Canadian Pacific 'Railway contract, which ought to have been broken long ago, and which could have been broken, not by repudiation but by investigation. It could also have been put an end to by negotiation. Since this government came to power, they have time and again given any number of concessions !to i the Canadian Pacific Railway :	but
they have never asked the Canadian Pacific Railway to consent to the repeal of that clause which enables the Canadian Pacific Railway to keep up their rates. We may be building a great transcontinental railway system ; it may be a fine thing for the right hon. gentleman to found a reputation on : that John A. built the Pacific railway, and he built a bigger one. That >may be, but it is not a solution of the transportation problem. It may be a Laurier monument, but that is all. The amendment proposed by the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Roche), is on the right lines, and if it be put into effect, it will place the Intercolonial Railway right in touch with the Northwest; it will build up the ports of the maritime provinces and it will be a step in the direction of giving that relief which the people of the Northwest are asking for.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
When the Minister of Justice suggests that something equivalent to this four years' clause may be enforced by means of control given by one of the sections of the agreement, he hardly does justice to the position in which the government finds itself. Eight years are given for the completion of the western division, and let us assume for a moment that the Minister of Justice is right in his opinion, that there is no legal liability imposed by the terms of clause 36 of the original agreement. There is an obligation of some kind imposed by that agreement, I would suppose ; and if the Grand Trunk Pacific Company proceeds to build this line so that in ordinary course it will complete it in eight years, and if it proposes to issue bonds for the purpose of enabling it to proceed, I do not see how any government could very well withdraw from what is at least a moral obligation under the terms of section 36, so far as the guarantee of the interim bonds is concerned. I do not think the country could expect very much relief from the minister's argument. Then, there is one circumstance that strikes us all through in considering the terms of this contract, especially the supplementary contract ; that is, that the obligations of the government are in a definite form-the hard, distinct form of actual contract-whereas the interests of the country are safeguarded merely by hopes and expectation. For example, the Minister of Justice says he hopes, believes, expects, that the prairie section will be completed in perhaps half the time allowed for the completion of the whole western division. Why should the interests of the country be preserved only by hopes and expectations-only by what the minister calls the business interests of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company ? Why, on the other hand, in sharp contradistinction to that, should every obligation in favour of the Grand Trunk Company or the Grand Trunk Pacific Company be absolutely safeguarded by the most distinct and positive agreements ? One would think the interests of the country had as much claim to be safe-

guarded as those of the corporations to which I have referred. So far as the completion of the eastern division is concerned, our position on this side of the House, as my hon. friend who has just sat down has said, is that the interests of the maritime provinces would be very much better conserved, in the matter of securing a portion of the western traffic, by the extension of the Intercolonial to the shores of the Georgian bay, and eventually to Winnipeg and the Pacific coast, than by any efforts directed towards the building of a railroad from Winnipeg to Quebec and Moncton through the northern portions of Ontario and Quebec. That has been repeated so often on this side of the House that it is not necessary for me to elaborate it any further.

Mr. Chairman, the amendment under consideration, if not the most important proposed to this measure, is one of the most important amendments. To my mind time is the essence of the whole Bill. When this railway was first suggested, we were told that traffic in the Northwest was congested, and that relief for the settlers was most urgent, in order that they might be enabled to move the products of their farms to the markets of the world. We well remember how hon. members from the Northwest appealed to this parliament time after time for relief for the settlers, pointing out how their grain was practically rotting in the fields for the want of adequate railway facilities. If a new railway is to be of use to the people of that country, it should be constructed with the least possible delay. Surely it does not require eight years to provide a remedy which these hon. gentlemen told us should be provided immediately. We cannot for a moment conceive that a rich corporation, having the directorate of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, backed up by the guarantee of the Dominion of Canada of 75 per cent of the money required to construct the road through the prairie section, and the guarantee of the other 25 per cent by the Grand Trunk Railway Company, requires a delay of eight years, from a financial point of view. There must be some other motive animating the government in proposing that the time for completing the road be extended for a further period of three years. It is not in the interest of any part of the country. If the road is a necessity, it should be constructed without any delay whatever. When the First Minister introduced the ' Bill for the construction of this road in the session of 1903, ' immediately ' was the word he used to denote when the work should be Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
undertaken and brought to completion. We hear nothing more of that now. They seem to have dropped the idea that it was an immediate necessity, and they are prepared to allow the people who were suffering in the Northwest to suffer still year after year ; and I am sorry to say that hon. members from the great Northwest sit in their places in this House dumb as oysters, and without protest allow this Bill to go through. But what are we to think when we look across the House and find, when we are considering a great transcontinental railway scheme involving an expenditure of from $150,000,000 to $170,000,000, that the Minister of Railways is not in his place ; the Finance Minister is not in his place, the First Minister is not in his place ; the Minister of the Interior, who should ever have a watchful eye over all legislation affecting the Northwest, is likewise not in his place ; and this matter is, for the present, relegated to the hon. gentleman who has charge of the fisheries down on the Atlantic coast.
I would like to know what connection there is between the Fisheries Department and the Transcontinental Railway. But this great scheme is relegated to a minister who is not supposed to have any connection with the undertaking. The hon. member for Marquette (Mr. W. J. Roche) has so clearly explained the amendment he proposes, and has gone so fully into the reasons why it should be adopted, that it is unnecessary for me to speak at length on the subject. I need hardly say that I support that amendment without hesitation. I hope that the government, led by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, will take this matter into its serious consideration, and will not allow the completion of this prairie section to be postponed for eight years and so deprive the people of that country for such a long time of the benefits of additional railway communication. In my opinion, another transcontinental railway will be demanded for that country before this term of eight years expires. Why should these delays be allowed ? Are they in the interests of the Grand Trunk' ? Are they in the interest of the Grand Trunk Pacific ? Surely the government, with all its resources is able to complete the eastern division, which they have declared time and again they are going to do. Why, then, delay the western division. To my i-ind the construction of the eastern division is not of the greatest importance unless the western division is completed also, because the western division is to feed the eastern. I say again that I hope the government will seriously consider this question and accept this amendment in the interest of the people of Manitoba and the Northwest Territories, notwithstanding the fact that hon. members from that section are sitting here dumb as oysters and not uttering a

word of protest or making any effort to secure a more speedy construction of tlie road. I hope the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, representing the government, will give us some reason to hope that the amendment will at least receive the serious consideration of the government before it is voted upon.

transcontinental project. What is being done to promote that great scheme is being done in spite of these men and their friends, in spite of that company which to-day holds the Northwest Territories in the hollow of its hand, and which these hon. gentlemen are anxious should continue to control our country and help them back to office. But the people of the Northwest are not to be deceived. We have suffered too long from the policy of hon. gentlemen opposite and the monopoly of the Canadian Pacific Railway. We have suffered too long from the administration of hon. gentlemen opposite and the railway monopoly on which they have prided themselves for so many years. Had they, in the beginning of this proposition, said, ' yes we welcome some means, any means of relieving that country from monopoly ; had they put forward some alternative proposition worthy of consideration ; had they adopted the policy of government ownership, had they adopted any policy but the policy of obstruction, they might have received some credit. But they did not adopt any policy except a policy of obstruction, and from day to day, during this session, their policy has been obstruction, obstruction, obstruction, and nothing else. What policy is contained in the amendment proposed by the leader of the opposition ? Only a policy of delay. What policy can you find in the amendment of my hon. friend from West Toronto ? Only a policy of delay. And that policy has been backed up from day to day with only ten, twelve, fourteen and possibly sometimes a few more members of the opposition in their places. This corporal's guard have been holding up this great transcontinental scheme simply by the parliamentary privilege of obstruction ; while an the time the great body of the members of the opposition were absent, transacting their business at home. A handful of them here in parliament have dared to face this country and hold up the government's transcontinental railway scheme in the. interests of monopoly. And now they hope to save themselves by a motion to limit the time for construction of the prairie section. An hon. gentleman near me suggests that if they would limit the time for debate, they would do something to facilitate the construction of this railway. I endorse his suggestion, and I put this view before the House, that every day hon. gentlemen opposite hold this bargain from completion is a day taken olf construction and added to completion of the railway. It is the deliberate purpose of hon. members of the opposition this session. as it was their purpose last session, to delay, and if possible block this scheme. They are working with that object; and their hope is this year, as it was last, that by delay and still further delay, something may yet turn up that may save their friends from ultimate competition and stop the Northwest from relief. Last year Mr. OLIVER.
their efforts were crowned with success. They held the House in session from day to day and from month to month until the snow flew and until the money market hardened and a season of lesser prosperity of the west reduced credit.
Oh, oh.

Yes, they did this so that this bargain, which was to be financed on the basis of money at three per cent, could not be financed on that basis. The whole basis of this Grand Trunk Pacific Railway bargain was that money could be borrowed at three per cent. It could when that bargain was made, but the money market tightened and the rate for money rose, and hon. gentlemen in touch with the money market conditions of London, through their friends of the Canadian Pacific Railway, knew that every day they were holding parliament in session and preventing the completion of the bargain was bringing them nearer to hoped for victory. That was their hope ; and last winter their friends throughout Eastern Canada chuckled to themselves and said, the bargain is dead and the Grand Trunk Pacific will never be built. But when this session opened they found the present bargain ready and the money deposited; and now their policy is to delay from day to day so as to prevent construction, and if they succeed as well for another month as they have during the past two, the summer will be half gone and construction will have become practically impossible for another year. That is what these gentlemen are working for. That is their general scheme, of which this amendment is but a part. Do they think we do not see these things ? Do they imagine we do not know them ? Do they believe that the people of the Northwest do not know and appreciate their manoeuvres at their full value ? The Grand Trunk Pacific put on its surveyors last September from one end of the Northwest to the other. They ran the surveys all winter ; never took their men out of the field, so that the line might be ready for construction as soon as this spring opened. When parliament sat on the 10th of March, the bargain was completed, the deposit was made, and the only thing lacking was the assent of this parliament. That was the 10th of March and we are now at the 10th of May. Two months of a session, none too long, already used up, and we have heard that our hon. friend's brag that another month will yet go before the bargain is assented to. Another month will carry us nearly to July, and practically the possibility of effective work this summer will be gone. And these are the gentlemen who want credit, who want praise, who expect to win votes throughout the Northwest, because they propose to limit the time for the construction of the prairie section.

I am glad indeed that I succeeded in drawing one hon. member

from the Northwest Territories out of his shell. I thought that these hon. members ' had forgotten that they represented that great northwest country as day after day ipassed, whilst this large measurt in the interests of that country was under discussion and we had never a word of counsel from them. The hon. gentleman says that we have been adopting a policy of obstruction.
Hear, hear.

Hear, hear, several hon. members say. I presume they are simply voicing the sentiment expressed by my hon. friend from Alberta (Mr. Oliver) -in no way sincere in expressing that sentiment however, because I am quite sure that this House and the country will endorse the statement I make when I say that no obstruction has been offered to the construction of a transcontinental railway in Canada. We on this side of the House have offered to the government a railway scheme, not to be completed in eight years, not to be completed in four years, but a scheme which would practically give immediate relief to the people of the Northwest and that is what makes my hon. friend from Alberta (Mr. Oliver) feel so bitter and so much out of temper as he is compelled to stand up behind the government and cast a vote contrary to his own convictions, a vote which he knows is not in the interest of the people whom he represents. It is beyond question that the people of the Northwest want a railway into that country in less time than eight years. On this side we are prepared to give them a railway in a mere fraction of that time, but the hon. gentleman who has talked so much about obstruction realizes the fact that he is compelled, as I said, to stand by the government which he is supporting and to refuse to the people who are so much interested in getting railway construction in there, and that puts him entirely out of temper so that he is unable to say anything but ' obstruction, obstruction.' The people of the west have no doubt been demanding railway construction. He says they have been demanding it for ten or fifteen years. Possibly they have. That is about as long as I have been in parliament and I am not going to quarrel with him about the time. But if they have been demanding additional railway facilities for ten or fifteen years, surely the hon. member will be satisfied to accept an amendment that would reduce the proposed time of eight years for the completion of a road through that country, to four years. Why does he not bring his tremendous influence to bear upon the government of the day and induce them to adopt a policy that would give more immediate relief to the people of that country ? Surely he is the man who is obstructing the people of the Northwest
by refusing to give them the necessary facilities which they are demanding. The hon. gentleman reflects on the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Roche) because he has proposed this amendment, has proposed an amendment that the road be constructed through the prairie section in four years instead of eight years. My impression is, and I think I voice the sentiment of every member in this House when I say, that the people of the Northwest will endorse the action of the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Roche) and condemn the speech of the hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver). What they want is immediate construction, and immediate relief. They do not want to be prevented from getting better railway facilities for a period of eight years if better facilities can be secured in four. Who will say it cannot be accomplished in four years ? Do you mean to say a great railway corporation with such an important directorate as is named in this Grand Trunk Pacific Bill-backed up, as I said before, by the whole Dominion of Canada, which furnishes three-quarters of the money, while the Grand Trunk furnishes the other quarter-who will say that a corporation like that is unable to construct a road through a prairie section of country for a distance of a thousand miles in four years ?
Nobody.
I am glad the hon. gentleman agrees.
They will do it in less time.

No one will agree to that, but the hon. member for Alberta condemns the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Roche) because he proposed a resolution which would reduce the time for the construction of that road from eight years down to four years. I am glad that I have one sympathizer, at any rate, on that side of the House and I hope when we come to divide on this amendment that the hon. member will not do like the hon. member for Alberta and vote against his own convictions, The Northwest wants railway construction ; we on this side have been and are now desirous of furnishing every facility at the earliest possible moment to relieve the congestion. We have offered a scheme and we claim it to be in the interests of the country if the government would adopt that scheme and give it effect. I trust that the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Roche) will receive the approbation of the government and the consent of this House.

I certainly would not occupy the attention of this House in reply to the observations made by the hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver) had it not been that I noticed that hon. gentlemen opposite seem to give a certain weight and authority

to his utterances, judging- by the applause *with which they greeted him. That hon. gentleman was complaining very bitterly that both last session and this the opposition of this House, had, as he expressed it, obstructed the passing of this Act. Thai is a rather serious charge and in my humble judgment it is a charge that is not only utterly unfounded, but is utterly unfounded to the knowledge of every gentleman opposite, and unfounded to the knowledge of the ministers. I rise in my place not to answer the hon. member for Alberta, not to waste time in discussing the question with him, but because I can see that he does not understand the meaning of obstruction. But at least he does understand the wisdom of the sage of old, who said :
He who fights and runs away
Lives to fight another day.
As his absence from the chamber amply demonstrates. But when we look at the agreement made last year between the government and the Grand Trunk, when we find that it was dated July 29, and therefore could not and did not reach this House until August, when this House had been nearly five months in session, when' we remember the work, apart from the Grand Trunk Pacific contract, that was then standing before the House, including the Franchise Act, which, so far as the individual members were concerned, was- one of the most important that could arise-when we remember these facts and remember when we adjourned, no one who understands the meaning of obstruction would accuse the opposition of obstructing this measure. Had the hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver) been in this House in 1896 when the Remedial Bill was before the House, he would have had a very different conception of the meaning of obstruction. I venture to suggest to hon. gentlemen opposite that obstruction would mean rising professedly to discuss a question, and not really discussing it but consuming the time of the House, saying nothing that could add to the information of the House or assist the House in arriving at a decision. If that be correct, I would ask hon. gentlemen opposite if any man ever rose in this chamber and more perfectly obstructed the business of this House than the hon. member for Alberta has done in the few moments he has occupied this evening. He rose to oppose a certain amendment, an amendment the object of which was to secure the building of the prairie section at as early a day as possible and I challenge any hon. gentleman opposite to state one single sentence, one single word, one single syllable that fell from his lips that had anything u*der the sun to do with the case before the House.

Not one word did he utter to show why an extension of time should be granted. He -did attack the opposition; he tried to flaunt tl^s, that and the other thing in the faces of the opposition, but on the question before the committee he had not a word to say. He was good enough to say-and I took his words down. We would like the bargain better than it is, but we are thankful to have it as it is. Why, Sir, he agrees with the opposition when he says: We would like the bargain better than it is. That is exactly the position we take on this side of the House. That is the position we took last year, that is the position we take to-day, but the difference between the hon. gentleman and ourselves is, that when we say that we would like to have the bargain better than it is, we do our best to secure a better bargain than the outrageous proposition which we now have before the House. freight rates on government roads are less than they are in Canada.

Government ownership in the Australian colonies, in New Zealand and the different countries of Europe has been a success. itself. How can you bring this Grand Trunk Railway to time in connection with the proposition that is now before the House ? to tlie employment of engineers for the making of these surveys ? His whole object is to evade the law. And, when you give him this $150,000,000 and this system of railways, he will be just as busy as ever trying how much he can take out of the people of Canada and how little he can give them in return. That is what he is paid for ; it is his business to work in the interest of his shareholders. The time has come when we want our railroad managers to work in the interest of the people of Canada and in some way to try and reduce the freight and passenger rates in the interest of the people. I venture to say that Mr. Hays and Sir Thomas Shaughnessy are working in the interest of the Americans who use our railroads. The Americans are getting the preferred rates to-day in freight transportation and in passenger travel. The people of the American republic have the preferred position in regard to both these great railroads, and they always will have until we own the roads and regulate the tariffs. That is the great fact of state ownership-you are not bound by any contract to any person ; you are free, every day in the year and every hour in the day, to apply the remedy which the situation calls for. And you cannot foresee what is going to happen ; you cannot protect yourself against the future by any contract. You can protect yourself if you have your freedom. if you have the complete control, if you can do to-day what is necessary to ameliorate the conditions of to-day. Mr. Hays will do nothing for the people of the Northwest, Sir Thomas Shaughnessy will do nothing for the people of the Northwest, any more than they will do anything for the east, unless they cannot possibly avoid it. What they are apt to do is to do all they can for the shareholders of their several companies, and to antagonize the waterway system of this country on every possible occasion. They delayed the improvement of our canals-they are on record as having done that-and they will do it in the future. They will oppose the canalization of the country between Lake Superior and Winnipeg, though that canalization will probably be one of the greatest means of relief to the country that could be afforded. You create these great private interests, these two great corporations that will be free to combine at any time, and the result will be that you will be led to do nothing for the lelief of the people, but much for the strengthening of the corporations. Let us stop giving the people's money to these private corporations and begin putting that money into a project that the people can own and control. Let us put our money into a railway proposition that will work in with our waterways ; let us put our money into a railway proposition that will build up our own ports. What guarantee
have we that the Grand Trunk Pacific will not be used ultimately in the interest of LTnited States ports ? I ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) if there is any guarantee ? This Grand Trunk can pass into the hands of the Canadian Pacific Railway. The Dutch shareholders of the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Grand Trunk Railway may get together any day and sell out to American railroad interests. There is nothing that so endangers the future of Canadian nationality, there is nothing so prejudicial to the territorial integrity of Canada, as that our railroads are liable at any moment to pass into the hands of American railroad interests. It is nothing for the Vanderbilt interest, the Morgan interest, the Rockfeller interest to go on the London market and buy control of the Grand Trunk. And, if that is done, where are we then ? If that comes, we shall have to exercise the right of eminent domain and take over these roads. I hope we shall have that power left at least. But, if hon. gentlemen opposite keep on giving away, they may give away the right of eminent domain some day, and then we shall find ourselves hopeless. Let us stop once fpr all. If the people's money is to be spent for railways, let it be spent for the people's railway. Let us have a road that we can control at any moment and on which we can regulate the rates at any moment, a road that foreigners cannot take out of our hands. If we do that we shall begin to solve the problem of transportation, to give the people cheaper rates and better means of communication. And the effect of this will be that we shall have done something to build up the country. We shall be prepared, as I said this afternoon to spend money liberally in opening up our back country.
