Mr. Chairman, I propose to move an amendment to clause 7 by way of adding a subsection for the purpose of binding the Grand Trunk Railway Company by its corporate name as well as the Pacific Company to observe the objects sought by the Bill of last session as well as the Bill now before the House, and the agreements which these Bills respectively

confirm and more particularly in reference | to the carrying of freight by a Canadian route to and from Canadian ocean ports and at a favourable competing rate. The objects of the scheduled agreements and of both Bills are stated in the preamble to the original agreement. The preamble of the original agreement provided :
Whereas, by reason of the growth in population and the rapid development in the productiveness and trade of Canada and especially of the western part thereof, and with a view to the opening up of new territory available for settlement, both in the eastern provinces and in the west, and the affording of transportation facilities for such territory, and for other reasons, the necessity has arisen for the construction of a National Transcontinental Railway, to be operated as a common railway highway across the Dominion of Canada, from ocean to ocean and wholly within Canadian territory.
It will be observed, however, that the agreement of last year, and also the present agreement are made between His Majesty and the Pacific Company alone ; the Grand Trunk Company not being bound. However, by section 4 of the present Bill, the Grand Trunk Company is authorized to enter into with His Majesty, such contracts as may be necessary to carry the scheduled agreements into effect. Therefore when this Act shall have been passed the way will be open for making the condition which I propose should be made in connection with the aid which is given ostensibly, to the Grand Trunk Pacific, but in reality to the Grand Trunk Railway. In my humble opinion the somewhat lengthy discussion in this House last session and this session, has made the following points abundantly plain :	First: that the Grand Trunk Company and the Grand Trunk Pacific Company are one interest, are composed in fact of the same persons ; Second, that the company will complete the western division long before the government can complete the eastern division. In fact we have recently had the government's admission in this House, that the company for over a year have been actively engaged not only on the surveys of the western division which the company has to construct, but on that portion of the eastern division between Winnipeg and the North Bay connection. They have been doing that apparently with the assent of the government. We may adduce from this, the fact, that that section will be constructed long before the government can construct the eastern section, and the result of that will be that the Grand Trunk Pacific will send its freight either on their American connections by way of Chicago, or by its North Bay connection down by the main line of the' Grand Trunk through Montreal to Portland. Third : that these routes being established, the traffic will not afterwards be diverted, even when, if ever, the government
have completed the eastern section. Fourth : that it is the interest of the Grand Trunk, and will for all time remain their interest, to utilize these routes instead of the Quebec-Moncton-St. John route. Fifth : that the Grand Trunk Company will not consent to render useless and unproductive its expensive terminals at Portland. Sixth : that there is no evidence showing that it is possible to make a route for grain over the Winnipeg-Moncton section which will enable the company to haul grain at a profit, as against the water or rail and water route. Seventh : that there is no evidence showing that it is possible to build on the eastern division the high class of railway which it is admitted is the only class which could hope to compete with existing routes by water or by rail and water. Eighth : that there is in fact no evidence to show that it is at all possible to build the eastern division as projected. In order to show that the Grand Trunk Railway itself regards the two companies as one, and what the benefits are that the Grand Trunk Railway expect to receive, let me call the attention of the House to the language used by Sir Rivers-Wilson at pages 6 and 7 of the record of the proceedings of the meeting of shareholders of the Grand Trunk held on the 8th of last March. Sir Rivers-Wilson having described the enormous growth of the western country in population and wealth, and having dilated upon the necessity of the Grand Trunk, in their own interests, getting an entrance into that country, he proceeds :
There is no time to be lost if we are to avail ourselves of the great opportunities presented. Prosperity is flowing rapidly from the east to the tvest outside and beyond the territory covered by the Grand Trunk. Thus surrounded on all sides by elements of progress, it is absolutely impossible for our company to stand still. We must either continue to advance, or must recede and yield the offered advantages to more enterprising and far-seeing competitors. Having arrived then at the conclusion that the best interests of the company necessitated some early measure in the direction I have indicated, we caused a Bill to be introduced into the Canadian parliament for securing a charter of incorporation for the creation of a company with an independent organization, but in close connection with and under the control of the Grand Trunk Company for the purpose of building a line of railway from a point of junction at or on the Grand Trunk line, passing through the most fertile districts of the Northwest, and terminating at a port on the Pacific coast.
Further on he says :
Our original idea was to build from a point on the Grand Trunk Railway to the Pacific coast. The intention was that the point of junction should be at or in the neighbourhood of North Bay. It was made, however, by the government a condition of the grant of the charter of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company that a line should be extended eastward from North Bay to Quebec into the city of Moncton,

_ in New Brunswick, to the point of junction on the Intercolonial Railway communicating with St. John, New Brunswick to the southwest, and Halifax, Nova Scotia, to the southeast. As a result, however, of negotiations with the government, another Bill was introduced hy the government itself for ensuring the construction of the contemplated line from New Brunswick to the Pacific in joint partnership between the government and the Grand Trunk Pacific Company. An agreement under which this line would be constructed and worked was embodied in the government Bill, and it is the first of the two agreements which are submitted to you to-day so far as they affect the interest of the Grand Trunk Company. The Bills and the agreement were discussed hy paijiament during the whole of an unusually prolonged session.
Lord Wei by, speaking on the same subject, is reported to have said at page 20 :
The government of Canada has come to a provisional arrangement, subject to your approval, with the board. If you say ' No,' there is very little doubt that there are many others ready to avail themselves of the opportunity, and we have every reason to believe that the government of Canada has entirely decided that it will carry out this new line, and, if you refuse to do it then other parties, without any doubt, are ready to come forward and take up the development which is offered and the opportunity will pass away from you.
Mr. Hays, speaking in the same tenor, says (page 31) :
Now, gentlemen, the Grand Trunk Pacific is going to be in quite a different position from that of an ordinary new enterprise stretching across the territory I have explained to you. Here is the Grand Trunk, the parent company, standing with a large traffic ready to deliver it westbound. It does not have to wait five, ten or fifteen years to build up a traffic ; it starts with a traffic right from the beginning, and that of a most remunerative character, a high class traffic, consisting of agricultural material, dry goods, boots and shoes, and all that class of merchandise that a new and rapidly developing country requires. The Grand Trunk as it is to-day hauls it 200 miles and hands it over to a competitor and gets nothing back. Is that a businesslike position to be in ? Is that a position for the directors and management of the Grand Trunk to maintain and to acquiesce in ? I do not think you will say so. This enterprise -which we are advocating to-day, ladies and gentlemen, combines points and advantages that no other transcontinental line in the United States or Canada can have.
Therefore I think it is abundantly clear, from these statements of the railway interests, that they speak of themselves as one and the same interest, composed as they are of the same people ; and they refer to the benefits that are to accrue from the scheme as benefits to the Grand Trunk Company. That is the state of affairs as between the government and the railroad interests. We have the Grand Trunk Company, in no way bound to carry out the scheme as it has been presented by the government to this House, and under no obli-Mr. ALCORN.
gation other than those provided in the two subsections of this section. We have, on the one hand, the Grand Trunk Company, a wealthy corporation, thoroughly responsible for all its engagements, whose covenants would be good, and the actual beneficiary under the scheduled agreements not bound in any manner whatever ; and we have on the other hand the Pacific Company, the mere legal entity, the technical myth, the artificial unreality, created by the government at the request of the Grand Trunk Company, for the purpose of assuming ail the liabilities, although, as has been admitted in this debate to-day, an unsubstantial company, without assets or credit. That company has never had any exigible assets, nor will it ever have any ; for all its property will be covered by the mortgages which under these agreements it must necessarily make to the government ; and when it will fulfil its obligation to purchase the necessary rolling stock, it will be without credit. It is that company, without assets or credit, that the government would have us accept as our sole security instead of the Grand Trunk Company which would be perfectly responsible for its engagements. At the same time, we have the evidence of a Grand Trunk officer that the whole of the benefits which are to accrue to the railroad interests from these agreements will go in fact to the Grand Trunk Company, which, as I have said, is in no way bound. Now, the absence of any such feature in this agreement so appeals to the business mind that we find our American cousins resident in Atlantic seaport cities, and with some understanding of this matter by reason of their connection with the Grand Trunk, which has its terminals in those cities, so struck with this fact that the Boston ' Advertiser ' in a recent issue has something to say about the Grand Trunk Pacific, and the government's claim that it will take Canadian goods to Canadian ports. It says :
While the Laurier government talks about the use of Canadian ports by this road New England is not alarmed. The new road, when built, must hand its freight over to the Grand Trunk, and the latter will carry the freight wherever there are the most steamships to take it. It is true that the Canadian government has signed contracts with the new company to have the Canadian ports used as much as possible, but the new company does not control the entire haul. And when the cars switch from the road of the Grand Trunk Pacific to the Grand Trunk, the latter has the say as to the destination, in many cases. If the New England ports have the best facilities, the biggest fleets, the road will do its best to work along that line. The export business is not a matter of sentiment. The very fact that no contract has been made binding the Grand Trunk in the future is a pretty good sign that the Canadian government is building the new eastern line rather to catch votes than with much idea that the export business will be taken away from the ports of this section for very long.

It appears to me that the scheduled agreements and the Bills which severally confirm them, are one long record of concessions in money and credit to the allied companies. Canada, as regards the eastern section, pays all the cost and takes all the risk. If she succeeds ill building the line, she hands it over to the railroad interests for ten years free, and they may at any time abandon it and throw it back on our hands in a dilapidated condition. That is shown bv the fact that the contract as presented to the House contains no penalty in case the company sees fit to take that course. It is true, we have the covenant of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company that they will not adopt such a course ; but we have not the covenant of the Grand Trunk Company. Nor have we any penalty attached to the Grand Trunk Pacific Company if it should adopt such a course. Even if the eastern section is built, or if, as is more likely, it is not built, (except the North Bay section), or if the trade routes are established, as I have pointed out. what would happen '! Whichever course is taken, the Grand Trunk, by its American connections through Chicago or by its connection through the old main line eastward via North Bay, will reap all the benefit of the entire scheme if it is successful, and Canada will suffer all the loss if it proves a failure. Finally, let us observe that the government insists on providing by law that the Grand Trunk Company shall control the Grand Trunk Pacific. We have that specific provision made in these Bills. On the other hand, the opposition propose that the Grand Trunk Company shall come into this agreement by its corporate name-shall be absolutely and strictly bound to carry out the objects which the government ostensibly have in placing this scheme before the House, and shall use its best endeavours, notwithstanding its divergent interests, to carry on the trade through Canadian routes to Canadian ocean ports at fair competing rates. It is impossible for me to perceive any intelligent reason why the government should refuse to accept such an amendment as I have the honour to present, unless it be as has been alleged, that the government finds itself in the hollow of the hand of the Grand Trunk Company. If the government are able to offer any intelligent reason why this amendment should not be accepted -why the Grand Trunk Company, instead of the myth, the unreality, the company without assets or credit, should not be bound, I certainly have some curiosity to hear them.
I have the honour, then, to move, seconded by Mr. Wilson :
That section 7 of the Bill he amended by adding thereto the following subsection as subsection ' D.' :
Notwithstanding anything in this Act or in the Act hereby amended, or in the scheduled agreements contained, His Majesty the King acting as aforesaid, shall not be bound or obliged to perform, carry out or fulfil any of
ihe covenants, conditions or stipulations in the said scheduled agreements contained on behalf of the Dominion of Canada, unless and until the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada shall have entered into an agreement with His Majesty the King acting as aforesaid, by which the said Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada shall covenant and agree as follows :	That neither the Grand Trunk Pacific
Railway Company nor the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada shall in any manner within its power, directly or indirectly, permit, advise, or encourage the transportation of traffic by routes or at rates other than those provided in the said agreement, and that each of the said companies shall, in all respects and in good faith, use its utmost endeavours to fulfil the conditions upon which public aid is granted and accepted, namely, the development of trade through Canadian channels and to Canadian ocean ports.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have not bad an
opportunity of considering this amendment, as I have not had a copy of it, but I perceive from what I have heard that it proceeds on the assumption that the Grand Trunk Railway will be interested in ruining the earning capacity of the Grand Trunk Pacific, that the desire of the Grand Trunk Railway will be to divert trade from the Grand Trunk Pacific at Winnipeg down its American system by way of Chicago. But there are difficulties in the way. In the first place, there are no connections that I know of at present which would enable the Grand Trunk Railway to go from Winnipeg to Chicago. There are no lines existing now controlled by the Grand Trunk Railway which would enable that idea to be carried out. and no such line can be built except with the consent and sanction of the parliament of Canada. In addition, the project originally put forward by the Grand Trunk Railway; and upon which so much stress is laid by our lion, friends opposite-a project which appeared to receive the almost unanimous approval of these gentlemen-was to extend their line from North Bay into the city of Winnipeg, so as to put their Canadian system in touch with the west. That project of the Grand Trunk Railway received the approval of hon. gentlemen opposite, but how could that be carried out if the Grand Trunk Railway are going to divert the trade down to Chicago ? In that case what will become of the connection between Winnipeg and North Bay ? Then we must not forget that the Grand Trunk Railway guaranteed the second issue of bonds. But if they ruin the earning capacity of the Grand Trunk Pacific, how will they meet the interest on that second issue ? In addition the Grand Trunk Railway will be the holders of the majority of stock in the Grand Trunk Pacific, and that stock they will have to pay for as hon. gentlemen opposite will no doubt perceive when they give the matter a little calm reflection. But when the Grand Trunk Railway' have paid money for that

stock, is it likely that tliey will proceed deliberately to ruin the earning capacity of the enterprise in which the}' hold the stock? It seems to me that all these reasons should induce us to reject the amendment offered by my bon. friend.

As I understand it, ffie object of the amendment is this :	Very
substantial aid has been granted by the country to this Grand Trunk Pacific, upon the understanding that the Grand Trunk Pacific will in good faith use its utmost endeavours to fulfil the conditions upon which such aid is granted, namely, the development of trade through Canadian channels to Canadian ocean ports. The clauses of the contract which purport to ensure the carrying out of that understanding are mere covenants of the Grand Trunk Pacific, but that company, as has been said so often during this debate is a mere figurehead, a nonentity in every respect, a company in mere name, a company whose policy is controlled absolutely by another corporation, a company which is absolutely in the power of another corporation, a company whose interests may not be those of the controlling body. Therefore we desire that that company which is given control shall itself be bound to do what its creature the Grand Trunk Pacific has agreed to do. It is of no avail to the country that the Grand Trunk Pacific should be under obligation to send this traffic in a partieu! ir direction, if the company which we place in control of it is itself free to do as it pleases in that regard. We say it is absolutely useless to make one company agree to do a particular thing, if it is to be bound by another company which may make it do the opposite. The Grand Trunk Pacific is bound not to divert traffic from Canadian to United States ports, but the Grand Trunk pacific is rendered absolutely helpless, because its whole policy is placed in the hands of another corporation ; and as that other corporation is the one which will reap the whole benefit, it ought to be bound to do that which the Grand Trunk Pacific agreed to do. Surely the Minister of Justice would not stand up and say that that is an unreasonable contention. If it were reduced to the case of individuals, the hon. gentleman would scout the idea of saying that the party who was to control the other should not himself be bound.
Could one imagine a more absurd proposition to be advanced by business men in the face of the millions of obligations this country has undertaken ? The Grand Trunk Railway Company is having put into its hands, into its grasp of iron, the whole of that immense property-3,400 miles of railway costing about $170,000,000, and we are to be satisfied with a mere covenant of a company subject to its control. The government refuses to consent to the con-Mr. FITZPATRICK.
trolling company being bound ; the government refuses to say that the Grand Trunk, which receives the whole benefit of this subsidy and guarantee, shall be bound to see done what they say the Grand Trunk Pacific must do ; we have to rely simply upon the covenant of a company that cannot control itself. Surely, the proposition need only be stated for its absurdity to be seen. The amendment moved by the hon. member for Prince Edward (Mr. Alcorn) is a plain business proposition that no man dealing between individuals would for a moment hesitate to adopt. I venture to say there is not a solicitor in the land but would insist upon such a covenant as is proposed here. What earthly use to this country is the covenant of the Grand Trunk Pacific that it will not divert the traffic when you put over its head another company that can make it divert the traffic whether it wants to or not? Of what avail will it be to have a covenant from the Grand Trunk Pacific that it will carry traffic to St. John or Halifax if another company can say the traffic must not go there ? Now, Sir, I do not wish to occupy unnecessarily the time of this House. I have had to speak on this subject far more frequently than I would wish to do. But I cannot understand how hon. gentlemen opposite-able men and honourable men as they are-and knowing, as I do that they must see the absurdity of many of these provisions-can sit in their seats, and vote down our amendments, the Grand Trunk Company may object to them. That is the position tliey occupy. Hon. gentlemen, on the Treasury benches, who know as well as I do, and believe as firmly as I do, that many of these covenants are mere fictions, sit there and call upon their supporters to vote down amendments that are proposed here, not on the merits of these amendments, but lest this agreement should fail, with political consequences that might be serious for hon. gentlemen opposite.
Amendment (Mr. Alcorn) negatived.

I beg to move :
That the Bill be amended by adding thereto the following section :-
The government shall have the right to inspect all books of accounts, statements, contracts, correspondence, vouchers, waybills, and all other papers and documents of ,the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada, the inspection of which may be considered necessary for the purpose of investigating or determining any question, matter or thing arising out of the said scheduled agreements, or the said lease, of the provisions of this Act or of the Act hereby amended, or connected with the apportionment of rates and earnings, or with the obligations or undertakings of the Grand Trunk Company or the Pacific Company, pursuant to the said agreements or lease, or to the National Transcontinental Railway Act or to this Act.

I think the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fitzpatrick) will concede that it is only necessary to state in a few words the object of this amendment to make its importance perfectly apparent. The hon. gentleman knows that there is no provision in the agreement or in the Bill itself by which it is possible to provide any machinery to investigate the relations between the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company and the Grand Trunk Railway Company. As has been already pointed out on many occasions in this House, these are one company lor all practical purposes. The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company exists only for the interests of the Grand Trunk Railway Company. Now, let me give some cases that will occur in the relationship between these corporations two in name but one in fact.
Let me take the case of the rentals to be paid for the last three years of the ten years on the eastern division. That will be governed entirely by the capabilities of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company to pay. It would be a very easy matter, and it would be somewhat businesslike on the part of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, to see to it that, by the division of the earnings between themselves and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company as managed by them it should be impossible for the Grand Trunk Pacific to pay the rental provided for under the provisions of the agreement. Then, let us remember that, with regard to the western section, this same thing would arise there. We have the western section controlled by the Grand Trunk Railway Company in the name of the Grand Trunk. Pacific Railway Company. AVe have the eastern connections from North Bay to Montreal and Portland owned and controlled by the Grand Trunk Railway Company having the Grand Trunk Pacific as a feeder.
In a word. Mr. Chairman, the object of this amendment is to secure means of investigating the relations between the Grand Trunk and the Grand Trunk Pacific. It is not a case where any one could interfere between two corporations under separate names and separate interests, but two corporations having one interest, that being the interest of the Grand Trunk Railway. We have no means under the present agreement or the present Act to examine into the accounts of the Grand Trunk Railway Company. They may milk the cow as dry as can be, every dollar of earnings that should go to pay the rental in the one case and interest in the other, can be absorbed by the Grand Trunk proper and we have absolutely no power to investigate or examine into the books or the accounts of the Grand Trunk. In a word the object of this amendment is one of which I am sure every hon. member in the House will recognize the importance. The government of the
day have a contract with the creature, the mere shadow of the Grand Trunk, and we must protect our interests by examining the accounts of the Grand Trunk as well as of the Grand Trunk Pacific. I need not enlarge upon that question as I am sure that every hon. gentleman will see the importance of a provision of that kind in order to guard the public interest. We have a right to know what the accounts of the Grand Trunk are and to know the relationship between the two companies, because we are concerned in aiding the Grand Trunk after all and the Grand Trunk should be brought within the reach of responsibility to the government. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Fitzpatrick), I imagine, unless I am greatly deceived, will be prepared to accept at least the substance of the amendment I have the honour to propose.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think I would be disposed to consider very favourably an amendment of this kind were it not that the essence of the amendment is provided for by the general Railway Act of last year, section 45 and section 49.

Do I understand the Minister of Justice to say that under the Railway Act the Board of Railway Commissioners can decide as between two railway companies what the relative proportion of their through earnings are?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not understand anything of the sort nor has my friend who has no doubt drawn this amendment any such idea. My hon. friend here will see that they have the right to inspect the books. Let him look at section 19 of the Grand Trunk agreement and he will there see that we have the power to investigate the books of the Grand Trunk Pacific.
For what purpose ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
For all purposes , to ascertain the proportion of traffic.
The company shall keep separate accounts of the earnings and expenditure of the eastern and western divisions, and, for the purposes of this agreement, the earnings from through traffic shall be apportioned between the eastern and western divisions.
Certainly.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Section 45 of the Railway Act provides:
The Governor in Council may at any time refer to the board for a report, or other action, any question, matter or thing arising, or required to be done, under this Act, or the special Act, and the hoard shall without delay comply therewith.
And section 49,
The board, the minister, inspecting engineer, or person appointed under this Act to make any inquiry or report may :-

Among other things
(d.) Require the production of all books, papers, plans, specifications, drawings and documents, relating to the matter before it or him.
That is only one company.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Where is the additional power here ?

The eastern and western divisions are to be operated by the Grand Trunk Pacific- and the provisions the hon. member refers to enables inquiry to be made as to the division of earnings as between the eastern and western divisions, a very proper and eminently business-like proposition. I would like the Minister of Justice to state when traffic goes over both the eastern and western division and also over the Grand Trunk proper, what provision he has made for ascertaining what division of the freights is made as between the three V I took some trouble to point that out last year to the hon. gentleman. The very fact that the hon. gentleman recognized that it was essential to our protection to have means of compelling a proper division as between the eastern and western divisions, shows that he requires a further provision to enable a propet apportionment to be made as between the Grand Trunk Pacific, both eastern and western divisions, and the Grand Trunk proper. Let us take traffic from say Edmonton to Montreal going over the western division to Winnipeg and over the eastern division from Winnipeg, to North Bay, then over the Grand Trunk proper-no party to these stipulations-from North Bay to Montreal. This agreement contains the provision that the government can intervene and see that the through rate is fairly and properly divided as between the western and eastern divisions as far as North Bay, and surely, as a matter of common sense, the hon. gentleman will see that a further provision is needed to settle the proper apportionment of the through rate as between these two divisions of the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Grand Trunk proper. If it were not necessary as against the Grand Trunk proper what was the object of having it here as between the two divisions of the Grand Trunk Pacific ? I think I made that very clear last year but' the trouble then was that if we altered so much as the dotting of an ' i ' or the crossing of a ' t ' in this agreement it would upset the whole agreement, and so hon. gentlemen would not listen to anything. Since then we have had the whole agreement thrown at large and the hon. gentlemen opposite have had opportunity to rectify all these omissions. The Grand Trunk, having one interest as to the western division and a different interest as to the eastern division, might unfairly divide the through rates so as to make the portion in which they have a leasehold interest non-paying, while the Mr. FITZPATRICK.
wsetern portion of which they hold dividend bearing stock would be made profitable, Therefore provision is made for fair apportionment. But that reasoning applies when you come to the through traffic running over the Grand Trunk to Montreal or to Portland, where the Grand Trunk might take for its share a higher proportion of the rate than was reasonable and so starve the Grand Trunk Pacific. We have not had a word from the minister upon that point. I would like to hear what the hon. gentleman has to say.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I was under the impression that this amendment had reference to the inspection of books ; I do not see anything else in it. Perhaps my hon. friend will read it again.
If the goverment had access to the books they would find out very soon if the rate was fairly divided.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is given by the Railway Act.

If the hon. gentleman thinks the clause is not quite sufficient he has his remedy. The hon. gentleman knows that in order to ascertain whether there is any unjust apportionment you must get at the books.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The Railway Act provides for it.
* Mr. BARKER. Why does the hon. gentleman, leave the Grand Trunk Railway Company in a position to take an undue proportion of the traffic to itself? Does the hon. gentleman dispute that it can do so? What control has he over the proportion that the Grand Trunk proper is going to take out of the through rate from Edmonton to Montreal or Portland? Does not the hon. gentleman know that the Grand Trunk proper is one corporation and the Grand Trunk Pacific is another and that the two may enter into an agreement for a division of the through rate by which one gets sixty per cent and the other forty per cent. That might be unreasonable, and yet it is quite lawful for these two companies to make such an agreement. The hon. gentleman says: Oh, you have not provided for that in this amendment. May I ask what is the duty of the hon. gentlemen opposite in such a case ? The difficulty is pointed out. I point out to them that on the face of this it is quite possible for the Grand Trunk Railway Company proper to take as its share of this traffic such a percentage of the through rate as will starve the leasehold portion upon which the government depend for its rent, and as may starve the western portion upon which the government has guaranteed the bonds. Yet, the hon. gentleman has provided no remedy for that. Is it not possible for him to look at it in the interest of the country? Is that the position that hon. gentle-

men on the treasury benches are going to take ? This amendment even in the minister's view of it, will enable the government to get at the facts and point out that an unreasonable advantage is being taken. But, supposing it does not, is the government going to sit still ? Is the government going to refuse to add words that will prevent the Grand Trunk Railway Company from depriving the government section of the road and the section which is guaranteed by the government, of its fair proportion ? It can take care of the traffic as between the eastern and western divisions. Why has it not protected the government against the Grand Trunk ? The point is that the Grand Trunk has an interest in depleting the traffic of the Pacific end for the benefit of its own road. The hon. gentleman says :	Oh, you have not provided
for that. What is the hon. gentleman going to do about it ? Is he going to sit still and ask the House to validate this agreement while leaving that blot upon it ? I should hope not. I should hope that even if a page of this House should whisper in the hon. gentleman's ear the possibility of such a thing, he would jump up instantly and take care of the interests of the country. Is there any reason why the hon. gentleman should not go as far as this amendment goes? Is there any reason why the hon. gentleman should not have the means of ascertaining whether a wrong is being done or not. The hon. gentleman will not even suggest his remedy for it. What is his remedy? The only provision that the hon. gentleman makes is as between the two sections of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. He leaves the Grand Trunk Railway open to do as it pleases. It is like three men entering into an arrangement under which two of them are bound as between each other and the third is left loose. Hecan-rob them both. That is the position the government has left this contract in. The Grand Trunk proper, an absolutely independent party, can take out of one hundred cents of earnings, sixty cents and leave twenty cents to each of the other two, and there is no remedy. The hon. gentleman has not provided one. He has taken very good care that the forty cents shall be divided fairly as between the two, but he has taken no precautions as against the Grand Trunk Railway Company which controls the whole lot and will take what it pleases. I do not know anything that puts this government in a more ludicrous position as a government of business men than that. Even suppose this amendment were subject to the doubt which the hon. Minister of Justice seems to east upon it, it would not leave the matter in as bad a position as that in which it now is.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Fortunately hard words do not break any bones. Really we 102
must observe to some extent the rules of the House. My hon. friend the leader of the opposition has put into the hands of the hon. member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) an amendment to move. We want to deal with that amendment. The amendment provides simply for an inspection of the books. If my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker) wants to bring in something in regard to traffic arrangements we will deal with that. He has asked that there shall be some arrangement whereby the books of the Grand Trunk shall be examined. My answer to that is that the General Railway Act, sections 45 and 49, makes provision for what he asks us to do. Why waste our time beating the air about something that effects traffic arrangements? If my hon. friend from Hamilton wants to get at the traffic arrangements he knows perfectly well that no such traffic arrangements as he suggests could be made between these two companies without getting the approval of the board of Railway Commissioners. Such an arrangement would have no validity whatever.
Why ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Because the law says so.
Does my hon. friend mean to assert that two companies operating a through line cannot agree that one shall have ninety per cent and the other ten per cent if they please?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not say thaL I say that they cannot make an arrangement of that sort without coming to the board of Railway Commissioners and having it approved of.

Does the hon. gentleman mean to say that without the sanction of the board of Railway Commissioners two companies forming a through line cannot agree between themselves as they please about the proportion of the rates which each shall receive ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
You do ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
Well, I do not think there is any use of arguing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In the meantime let us deal with the amendment.

I understand the hon. Minister of Justice to state that two companies forming one line could not agree in any way without the approval of the board of Railway Commissioners. I would like to know if that is so ?

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
speechtext: Shall the section be adopted ?

There is no great hurry about this ; we want the hon. Minister of



Justice to answer. It it is necessary for me to stand on my feet in order to entertain the chairman, I shall take great pleasife in doing it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I made the statement and I reaffirm it now. Such an arrangement as that in order to be enforced would have to be approved by the Railway Commissioners.

It is a matter of every day agreement between two railway companies forming a through line, one railway having 25 miles, perhaps, of that through route and the other 500 miles, that the company having the 25 miles would receive Ifive times the amount per mile that the other would get.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The question is, as to whether they must have been approved by the railway commission.
If there are two companies forming a through line, the railway commissioners may decide what the through rate will be

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: You cannot collect a "cent on the railway without having the approval of the Board of Railway Commissioners, under an amalgamated agreement or any other agreement.

If there are two companies forming a continuous line, they may charge a through rate to be approved by the Boat'd of Railway Commissioners, but suppose that the through rate is one dollar one of them may take 99 cents and the other one cent.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If a third party suffers because of that, he can go before the Board of Railway Commissioners.
Will the Minister of Justice point me out any clause that will prevent the two companies dividing the through rate between themselves V

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend's argument has been that the Grand Trunk Railway and the Grand Trunk Pacific might make an agreement between themselves which would be detrimental to the people of Canada. So long as no person complains no one would have anything to say to the arrangements between the two companies, but when some one complains, the Board of Railway Commissioners step in to remecTy the evil if it'eShste: [DOT] -

The Board of Railway Commissioners come between the railway company and the toll payer. But suppose a through rate of a $1 is approved of, and one company takes 99 cents and the other company takes one cent, the Board of Railway Commissioners have nothing whatever to say to it. There is nothing in the Railway Act to prevent it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What has that to do with this amendment ?

I am answering the argument of the Minister of Justice that the Railway Act provides for it all. I point out to the Minister of Finance who is always so anxious for the public interest, that there is a blot in this contract and. we may fairly say to him and to the Minister of Justice, that they owe it as a duty to the people of this country to remove that blot. Does the Minister of Finance understand me ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What I understand is that the hon. gentleman is trying to show that there is a blot in his own amendment. He and his associates have prepared an amendment and they have persisted in talking about something else. I do not think that two such eminent jurists as the Minis ter of Justice and the member for Hamilton should show a bad example to the laymen of the House in straying away from the subject which is before us. We have had an opportunity of rambling over the whole contract again and again, and there is no need of doing it on this amendment.

I was not addressing myself to the Minister of Finance as a professional gentleman, but as a businessman, and I understand he plumes himself on being a man of business. This after all is a matter of -business, and it is a question whether the gentlemen sitting on the treasury benches are going to force through the clause as it stands now, because the Minister of Justice says amendment does not go far enough.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The amendment does not touch the case within one hundred miles.

Does the Minister of Justice mean to say that the difficulty we have been pointing out, and which we in our humility have been endeavouring to correct, is not a real difficulty ? Knowing that the difficulty exists, is lie going to force this agreement through and remain silent about it ? Is that the position of the hon. gentleman, and is this another case in which we must bow down before the Grand Trunk ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has been talking about a matter which is not referred to in the amendment, and which seems to have dawned on him since the amendment was proposed. We believe that this thing is provided for by the law. There is no traffic or tolls which can be levied on any railway in Canada without the previous sanction and approval of the Board of Railway Commissioners.
That is not the point at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In addition to that there can be no amalgamation agreement between two companies without the approval

of the Board of Railway Commissioners, and that is the point which we are dealing with, and if my hon. friend will read section 281 of the Railway Act he will find that that is the case. A railway company cannot collect anything on its own railway without the consent of the board, nor can it make an agreement with another company without submitting that agreement to the board.

Do I understand the Minister of Justice to say that it would be necessary for the Grand Trunk Railway and the Grand Trunk Pacific to submit this agreement to the Board of Railway Commissioners ? The Grand Trunk Railway in the supplementary a'greement is given control of the Grand Trunk Pacific.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We are dealing with freight rates now.
I am answering the statement of the Minister of Justice, that they cannot agree to anything without the approval of the Board of Railway Commissioners.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have not said anything of the kind.

Suppose the Board of Railway Commissioners approve of a rate between Edmonton and Montreal ; the division of that rate between the Grand Trunk Railway and the Grand Trunk Pacific is a matter of agreement from day to day between the two companies. We propose that the government of Canada shall have power to inspect not merely the books of the Grand Trunk Pacific, eastern and western divisions, but the books of the Grand Trunk proper, so as to ascertain what the division of these rates may be. Then perhaps we will have the Board of Railway Commissioners to decide whether the agreed apportionment of the rates is reasonable or not, having regard to the interests of the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The Grand Trunk Pacific own And ornate the line from Win-nipi^weSF; the Grand Trunk Pacific operates the line from Winnipeg east. It is one through line operated by the Grand Trunk Pacific so far as regards its operation. In order to allow us to intervene in respect of that company, so far as its different rates over its own line are concerned, we have section 19, which enables us to inspect the books of the company with respect to the lines under its own control.
Why ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Because it is necessary to the subdivision of the rates between the government-owned and operated road and the company-owned and operated road. It is quite apparent that we must have that power to investigate if we want to be sure of the earning power of the com-1024	,
pany, and ascertain whether the three years' payments should be deferred or not. Dealing with the other proposition, as between the Grand Trunk and the Grand Trunk Pacific, say between the line of the Grand Trunk Pacific from Edmonton to North Bay and the line of the Grand Trunk from North Bay to Montreal, you are dealing with separate corporations. Neither the Grand Trunk nor the Grand Trunk Pacific can collect anything in the way of tolls or rates without submitting their tariff to the Board of Railway Commissioners. The Board of Railway Commissioners must first approve of the tariff on both roads. If the Grand Trunk Pacific enter into an agreement with the Grand Trunk, what is called a traffic arrangement, the Board of Railway Commissioners must examine that agreement, and it cannot take effect without the approval of the board.
The Minister of Justice has either not listened to me or I have failed to convey my meaning to him.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have not listened.

I am sure the hon. gentleman could not have failed to understand me if he had listened. He must know that every hour of every day throughout the year through rates are made all over the continent. It may be from San Francisco to Portland or from Chicago to New York. The companies can all agree by telegraph, from hour to hour probably in exciting times, what their through rates shall be, and what the divisions of those rates shall be. No authority controls what each may take of the through rate. The commissioners decide what the whole rate shall be. That is what affects the shipper. What we are trying to get at is that the Grand Trunk proper, controlling the whole affair, shall not be in a position to. take more out of the through rate for its own rails than it allots to the government-leased portion or to the western division. That question has nothing to do with the amount of the through rate. The Board of Railway Commissioners will see in the Shippers interest that the through rate is not more than is right. That is not the question we are dealing with. It is the question of dividing the through rate between the three sections-the western division, the eastern division and the Grand Trunk proper ; and it is just as material in the interest of this country, as lessors and guarantors, to have control over that apportionment as it is the interest of the lines of the Union Pacific and its connections from San Francisco to New York, to know what their divisions are, so that they will each get their fair share of the lawful rate ; and the hon. gentleman should protect the country in that respect here. If the Grand Trunk choose, it can take the lion's share of every through rate which the Board of Railway Commissioners may authorize.

I desire to ask tlie Minister of Justice one question. I suppose I ought to make an apology. I ask the question with that proper humility which laymen ought to have on all such questions. Assuming that every agreement between railway companies with regard to traffic rates must first be approved by the Railway Commission, I will suppose that the Railway Commission fix a certain rate from Edmonton to Montreal. That is to be divided between the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Grand Trunk Pacific. Would they assign a certain proportion of that rate to the one and a certain proportion to the other 7 I do not think they would. They would inquire if that was a fair rate-why ? In order to protect the shipper from paying too much. We will suppose that the next time the shipper ships over the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Grand Trunk, and he pays the same rate. Does the hon. gentleman say it is necessary to protect the shipper in the one case more than in the other, and that it is necessary to interfere with the two corporations as to the division of the rate ? The hon. gentleman would say :	No, they
may divide it as they please, because we have taken care that the shipper is protected. The shipper is protected in the same manner in the one case as in the other. So that it does seem to a layman as stupid as myself that there is no protection such as is sought by the amendment, namely, that the government shall have the right, not on behalf of the shipper, but on behalf of the whole people of Canada, who are backing this scheme, to see that the division of these rates is properly made. If there is any doubt about it, surely we ought to avail ourselves of the opportunity to correct any difficulty of that kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend is far too modest in his estimate of himself. I am sure that no man would be more surprised if we took him at that estimate than himself. We are dealing with an amendment which provides for, the inspection of the books. I have pointed out, I think to the satisfaction of some hon. gentlemen opposite, that the General Railway Act provides for that. We have travelled from that amendment to another ground-that respecting the division of the freight rates as between the two companies, and the hon. gentleman says : Assuming that the tolls levied were fair on the whole route, and the shipper would not have a right to complain, what would the Railway Commissioners do ? I am not here to declare what the Railway Commsisioners would do.
The hon. gentleman has assumed what they would do ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend will bear me out that I have not assumed anything except to point out what Mr. BARKER.
the law is. I will venture, however, to assume what I would do if I were a railway commissioner. If I felt an agreement of this sort was entered into so that the public interest would be jeopardized, I would think the government would have the right to go before the Railway Commissioners and complain of that agreement in precisely the same way as a private individual would.

I would ask the Minister of Justice to point out one word in the Railway Act which enables the Board of Railway Commissioners to make any investigation into the apportionment of the rates and earnings as between the railway companies There is nothing to prevent the companies giving the whole through rate, whatever U may be, to one of them if they choose. The

Grand Trunk Railway can do what it pleases. It may give all the earnings to the Grand Trunk Pacific or take them all itself, or it may apportion them at its own pleasure, having the control of both companies, and that may make an enormous difference as to whether one section of the line may be profitable and another unprofitable.' There is nothing to enable us to investigate matters connected with the apportionment of the rates and earnings as between the Grand Trunk Railway and the Grand Trunk Pacific and this amendment goes beyond the Railway Act in giving such power of investigation.
Amendment (Mr. Clancy) negatived.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the clause be adopted ?

Before the clause passes, let me draw attention to clause 34 of the scheduled agreement, which provides that the Grand Trunk Railway shall guarantee the bonds of the Grand Trunk Pacific for the balance required for the construction of the western division. Clause 34 provides for two issues of bonds. Under this agreement the two are made pari passu.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not think that is quite correct.

It is for the balance required for the completion of the western division. I notice that under the Act giving the charter to this company they have only the right to issue $50,000 of bonds per mile. Does this clause empower them to issue more ? Because from the arguments I have heard here and the statement of the president of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, I am led to believe that it will require more than $50,000 a mile for the mountain section. How are you going to provide for this ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The point raised by my bon. friend is, I suppose whether or not the Grand Trunk Pacific charter, which authorizes the issue of the bonds, authorizes the company to issue bonds to the extent of $50,000 a mile for the mountain section and $20,000 a mile for the prairie section, will be construed as being extended by this agreement
Does the hon. gentleman think this empowers the company to issue for more than $50,000 per mile ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I would not like to say that.

We would like the section to stand, but the amendment is rejected.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext: I think we ought to have some explanation showing why this exception to the rule should be allowed.

A similar measure has already been proposed with regard to other insurance companies to meet the conditions arising from losses incurred in the Toronto fire. The Ottawa Insurance Company desire to reduce their capital stock in order to meet the difficulties incurred-
But is this not a petition to incorporate a company ?

The company is already incorporated under Act of the Ontario legislature, and it now seeks incorporation under this authority in order to meet the difficulty that has arisen and so that it may not be necessary to wait until next year.
